Pulled the code — and the honest answer is **we never wired an IP-octet salt; it's still the fixed string `WG-STABLE-PSK-2024`** in `wireguard_auth.rs`. The only octet logic that exists (`op-core/src/security.rs:312-328`) is network-*prefix* masking for ACL matching, not salt derivation. So this is a decision to make now, not recover.

Between your two options, **last 2 octets** is the right one — and the reasoning is decisive, not a toss-up:

| | First 2 octets (e.g. `10.100`) | Last 2 octets (e.g. `0.2`) |
|---|---|---|
| What they are | the **network/plane prefix** | the **host portion** (the peer's slot) |
| Across peers | **identical** for everyone on the subnet | **unique per peer** |
| As a salt | ❌ defeats the purpose — a shared salt is no salt | ✅ unique-per-identity, which is exactly a salt's job |

A salt's whole job is to be **unique per identity** so two users with the same input don't derive the same key (and to kill rainbow-table reuse). The first 2 octets are shared by every peer in the plane → useless. The **last 2 octets are the per-peer unique part** → correct.

Two caveats that matter for it to actually work:

1. **Must come from the *stable assigned* IP, not a live/ephemeral one.** You deliberately made the PSK stable so peers don't get locked out mid-session — same rule here. Salt it from `assigned_ip` in `privacy_routes.json` (the permanent `/32` allocation), never from whatever IP the box currently has.

2. **Last-2-octets is only unique within a /16.** `10.100.0.2` and `10.200.0.2` both have last-2 = `0.2` → salt collision across planes. If your peers ever span multiple second-octets, two different users could collide. Cheap fix: salt with the **full `/32`** (all four octets) — still IP-derived, still stable, but globally unique in your space. Same idea you're after, no collision.

So my recommendation: **salt = the host portion of the stable assigned IP, ideally the full `/32`**; if you want literally 2 octets, make it the **last** 2.

One thing to decide so I can log it: do you want the salt to be **just the last 2 octets** (collision-risk across planes, but matches your memory), or the **full assigned `/32`** (same concept, collision-free)? You're right, and that kills MAC for this — WireGuard is L3 point-to-point, no Ethernet frames cross the tunnel, so the server **never sees the client's MAC at runtime**. It's only present at provision time (user-typed). Using it as a salt would mean the server stores it and trusts a claim it can't re-observe — exactly the privacy/verifiability problem we're trying to avoid.

So the constraint sharpens: **the salt must be something the server can independently see over WG at runtime.** Over the tunnel, that's basically two things — the **WG pubkey** and the **assigned `/32`**. Both stable, both unique, both mutually observed, and the pubkey is *cryptographically proven* by the handshake (not just claimed).

But there's a trap if you stop there: if the derived key is `Argon2(pubkey, salt=pubkey)`, then everything is a function of the **public** key → anyone who knows the pubkey recomputes the "secret." No actual secret. You need one secret input the server can verify but an attacker can't supply.

That secret is your **PSK** — and here's the nice part: WireGuard has a **built-in preshared-key slot** (`PresharedKey` in the config) that's a symmetric secret mixed into the handshake. Your `--psk` field maps straight onto it. So the clean construction:

```
derived_key = Argon2( secret = PSK , salt = WG_pubkey )
```

- **Salt = WG pubkey** — server-observable over WG, unique, stable, handshake-proven. ✓
- **Secret = PSK** — the real secret; server stores only `blake3(psk)` to verify, never raw. ✓
- **MAC** drops out of the runtime path entirely — keep it (hashed) only as a provision-time hardware binding if you want, but nothing depends on seeing it over the tunnel.

That satisfies everything: only the user holds the real secrets (WG privkey + PSK), the DB stores public pubkey + a derived token + `blake3(psk)`, and the server can verify at runtime using only what it observes over WG.

content.text:
No — and this is the crux of the whole session-id question, so worth nailing:

**BLAKE (BLAKE2/BLAKE3) is deterministic. Same input → *same* output, every single time.** It's a hash, not a random generator. It looks "always different" only because you fed it something that changes.

That's exactly what was happening in the old design:

```
BLAKE2s(pubkey + timestamp)   → different each connection  — but ONLY because timestamp changes
BLAKE2s(pubkey)               → identical every time        — same input, same hash
Argon2(PSK, salt=pubkey)      → identical every time        — no changing input
```

So the "freshness" never came from BLAKE — it came from the **timestamp** mixed into the input. Remove the timestamp and it's the same value forever.

This decides your session-id question cleanly:

- **If `session_id = Argon2(PSK, pubkey)`** (what "session id = derived key" gives) → it's the **same value every session**. Stable, identity-bound. Not fresh.
- **If you want it to change per visit** → you *must* feed in something that changes: a **timestamp** (predictable, weak) or a **server-issued nonce** (the right answer — unpredictable and server-verifiable).

So the real fork is just: do you want the session id to be **stable** (= the derived key, simplest) or **fresh per visit** (= derived key **mixed with a server nonce** at connect)? The crypto won't make it "automatically different" — that's a choice about whether a changing input goes in.

Which do you want — stable identity-bound, or fresh-per-visit with a nonce?

content.text:
Good question — and it directly affects where I store `blake3(session_id)`, so let me answer it before finishing the code.

## What determines what goes to the Cozo graph

Three gates, in order — and the first is the one you built the taxonomy for:

**1. subid classification (the primary gate).** Gemma classifies every item by subid category (`src/prj/sch/mut/obs/evt/exp`). That classification *is* what decides graph placement and edge type — `mut` (mutation) becomes a state-change node edged to the session, `obs`/`evt` become event nodes, `sch` defines schema nodes, etc. The subid category determines **whether** it's a graph node and **how** it connects. This is exactly why Gemma owns subid + routing.

**2. Persistence + relational nature.** Cozo holds what must *survive reboot* and be *traversed relationally* — durable entities and the edges between them. That's the dividing line against the other two stores:

| Store | Holds | Lifetime | Determined by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cozo graph** | identity records, soul, domains, feature flags, **relationships** (container→identity→domain→event) | durable | subid says it's a persistent entity/edge |
| **sled** (`/dev/shm`) | current-session footprint, datestamp, mutation_index | ephemeral (current sled only) | runtime, checked per-request |
| **Qdrant** | vectors (semantic) + per-event trace_id records | durable, but vector/log shaped | needs similarity search or is an `evt` trace |

**3. Secret/PII filter.** Cozo stores **public + hashed** only — pubkey, `UUID v5(pubkey)`, `blake3(psk)`, `blake3(session_id)`. Never raw secrets; email only if the client is flagged.

## So the rule in one line
> **Gemma's subid classification decides if an item is a graph node and what it connects to; if it's a durable, relational, non-secret fact → Cozo. Ephemeral runtime state → sled. Vectors/event-traces → Qdrant.**

For the code I'm writing: `blake3(session_id)` is a durable identity fact (subid `src`/identity), non-secret → **Cozo**, written at provision. The live sled just carries the current session_id + footprint for the per-request check.

Want me to record this as the storage-routing decision in `SIGNALS.md` (it's the kind of thing that'll get re-litigated), then finish wiring the `Argon2(PSK, salt=pubkey)` session-id into `wireguard_auth.rs`?

content.text:
That's a meaningful upgrade to the model — and it resolves the verification tension we were dancing around. A **rubber stamp is applied by the authority, not the visitor.** So the handstamp isn't something the user derives alone — **Ghostbridge stamps it** with its own official mark at the door (A.N.N.A., the authorizing-official, does the stamping). That means there's an **issuer secret** — the rubber stamp itself — held by Ghostbridge and never exposed.

This is better, because it fixes the earlier problem cleanly:

- Earlier tension: if `session_id = Argon2(PSK, pubkey)` is fully user-derivable, it's not unforgeable; but if the server only stores `blake3(psk)` it can't recompute it.
- **With an official stamp:** the footprint becomes **keyed by the Ghostbridge issuer secret** — e.g. `footprint = HMAC(ghostbridge_issuer_key, session_id ‖ sled_state ‖ datestamp)`. 
  - Only **Ghostbridge can produce** the stamp (it holds the issuer key) → the user **cannot forge** it.
  - Ghostbridge can **verify** it (it has the key) → no need to store/recompute from raw PSK.
  - The stamp is **official** — it carries Ghostbridge's authority, exactly like a rubber stamp carries the venue's seal.

So the layers sharpen:

| Element | Who produces it | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `session_id = Argon2(PSK, pubkey)` | the **user** (from their secrets) | "this is who I am" — the claim |
| **the handstamp / footprint** | **Ghostbridge** (issuer key, at the door) | "officially admitted tonight" — the seal |
| datestamp | the sled | "which night" — currency |
| trace_id | per event | the receipt |

And it adds one key to the storage model we hadn't named: the **Ghostbridge issuer key** — server-side only, the literal rubber stamp. It never goes in Cozo, never in the sled payload, never to the user. It's the thing that makes the footprint *unforgeable*, and it's why A.N.N.A. is the **authorizing-official** — she's the only one who can stamp.

So `derive_session_id` (user side) stays `Argon2(PSK, pubkey)`, but the **footprint/stamp** in the sled becomes an **HMAC under the Ghostbridge issuer key**, not a plain hash. That's the line that changes in the interceptor/sled-write path.

Want me to record this (official stamp = HMAC under Ghostbridge issuer key; issuer key is server-only) and fold it into the implementation — `session_id` derivation user-side, footprint as issuer-keyed stamp server-side?

content.text:
Two separate things with two different homes — and the second question has a sharp answer:

## Where the issuer key (rubber stamp) goes
**Not Cozo.** Cozo holds public + hashed identity facts; a private issuer key is the crown jewel. It goes in the **encrypted key store / vault**, same place the WG private keys live — `op-gateway/src/encrypted_storage.rs` (Argon2-encrypted), referenced by handle. Your codebase already has the pattern: `op-blockchain/DESIGN.md` uses `"vault://op-dbus/privacy/hash-salt"`. So:

| Thing | Home | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Ghostbridge issuer key** (the stamp die) | vault / encrypted key store | private; never leaves the server; Cozo at most holds a `vault://…` **reference**, never the key |
| **the stamp value** (`HMAC(issuer_key, …)`) | sled (runtime) + Cozo record | it's a MAC, safe to store — having it doesn't let you forge new ones |

So the key that *makes* stamps is vaulted; the stamps it *produces* are storable anywhere.

## Can a field be ACL in Cozo?
**Not enforced natively — no.** Cozo is an embedded Datalog/relational engine; it has **no built-in column/row-level access control** (no Postgres-style RLS, no per-field permissions). It won't stop a reader of the DB from seeing a column.

**But** — and this fits your architecture perfectly — Cozo is a *graph* DB, so you **model ACL as data**: relations/edges like `can_read(role, field)`, `grants(stamp, scope)`. Cozo is *good* at representing the ACL graph. The **enforcement** then happens where it already belongs in your system: at the **D-Bus projection / interceptor (A.N.N.A.)** layer — "every mutation is an enforcement point." The mirror decides what projects to whom based on the ACL edges + OSCAL tags; Cozo just *stores* the policy graph, A.N.N.A. *enforces* it.

message.content: so there is going to be an identity vault and a user store (db)

content.text:
Exactly — two persistent stores with a hard boundary between them, plus the runtime tiers that derive from them:

## The two stores

**🔐 Identity Vault** — *secrets only.* The crown jewels, encrypted, server-only, never projected, referenced by `vault://` handle.
- Ghostbridge **issuer key** (the rubber-stamp die)
- Server-held WG private material / encryption keys
- Anything that, if leaked, lets you forge or impersonate

**📇 User Store (Cozo DB)** — *public + hashed records and relationships.* Queryable, traversable, projectable (under ACL).
- WG **public** key (canonical identity anchor)
- `UUID v5(pubkey)` MCP token
- `blake3(psk)`, `blake3(session_id)` — verification hashes
- soul / domains / feature flags
- the **ACL graph** (modeled as edges)
- email **only if flagged**

## The boundary rule
> **If having it lets you forge or impersonate → Vault. If it's public, hashed, or relational → User Store.** The User Store may hold *references* into the Vault (`vault://…`), never the secret itself.

## How the runtime tiers relate
The two stores are the **source of truth**; the fast tiers are **derived**:

```
🔐 Identity Vault ─(issuer key)─┐
                                ├─► sled (/dev/shm)  = current session: session_id + datestamped footprint (stamped via issuer key)
📇 User Store (Cozo) ─(records)─┘
                                └─► Qdrant           = vectors (semantic) + trace_id event records
```

- **Vault + User Store** = durable, authoritative.
- **sled** = ephemeral projection of "who's live right now," footprint stamped using the vaulted issuer key.
- **Qdrant** = derived search/accountability layer.

So at provision: secrets land in the **Vault**, records land in the **User Store**. At runtime: A.N.N.A. pulls the issuer key from the Vault to stamp, checks the presented session_id against the User Store hash, etches the sled, logs the trace to Qdrant.

We've now resolved a *lot* of architecture in this thread (key derivation, session model, temporal/sled, storage routing, two-store split, ACL). Want me to **consolidate all of it into one `docs/identity-architecture.md`** (the canonical spec, so it's not scattered across SIGNALS rows), and record the two-store decision — then get back to implementing?

message.content: so the session id will be stored in the vaoult and the db?

content.text:
No — and the distinction matters, so let me be precise: the **raw `session_id` is stored in *neither*.** Each store holds a *different representation*, and only one of them touches the session at all.

| Store | Holds re: session_id | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **🔐 Vault** | **nothing** | The vault is only for things that let you *forge/issue* — the issuer key, private keys. `session_id` isn't an issuing secret, so it has no business there. |
| **📇 User Store (DB)** | `blake3(session_id)` — the **hash only** | Enough to *verify* a presented session_id (`blake3(presented) == stored`), useless to an attacker who steals the DB. Never the raw value. |
| **sled (`/dev/shm`)** | the **raw** session_id, transiently | Only while the session is live; ephemeral, zero-copy, gone on reboot. |
| **user's machine** | recomputes the raw on demand | `Argon2(PSK, pubkey)` from their own secrets — they don't even need to persist it. |

So the rule holds: **the raw secret-ish value lives user-side + ephemerally in the sled; the DB keeps only its hash; the vault keeps only forging keys.**

Why not put raw `session_id` in the DB or vault? Because it's effectively a **bearer credential** — whoever holds the raw value can present it. Storing it at rest server-side would make a DB leak = account takeover. Storing only `blake3(session_id)` means a leaked DB reveals nothing usable, exactly like storing password hashes instead of passwords.

The one place the raw exists server-side is the **live sled**, and that's deliberate: it's in `tmpfs`, current-session-only, checked at zero-copy speed, and evaporates. That's the "current wristband on the wall," not a stored record.

So: **DB gets the hash, vault gets nothing, sled holds the live raw, user recomputes it.** Want me to lock this (session_id: hash-in-DB, raw-in-sled-only, never-vaulted) into the spec?

Now we're at the real crux, and your instinct splits exactly right along the two client tiers:

## The linkage only exists for clients that opt in
- **Privacy / GhostBridge clients:** the **key *is* the identity.** No person behind it, no email, no user↔key link. The pubkey stands alone — there's nothing to link, by design. No dilemma.
- **Corporate / compliance clients:** they **choose** to bind a real user to the key — because accountability/audit/non-repudiation is the thing they're buying. *They* create the dilemma by opting into it.

So "how do you link the user with the key" is **only a compliance-tier question.** Privacy clients never have it.

## What the join key is, and where the link lives
The **pubkey is the join** across stores — it's the one stable, public anchor present everywhere. Then for compliance clients only:

| Store | Holds (compliance client) | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **📇 User Store (DB/Cozo)** | edge: `pubkey → real_user` (PII), `pubkey → blake3(session_id)` | operational lookup + audit graph |
| **🔐 Vault** | the **sealed de-anon binding** — the user↔key link **encrypted**, openable only under authorization | lawful/compliance recovery, gated by A.N.N.A. |

This is where your "**in both**" instinct is correct — but it's not the *raw derived key* duplicated, it's two **different roles** of the binding:
- **DB** holds the *operational, queryable* link (hashes + the pubkey↔user edge) — used every request.
- **Vault** holds the *sealed escrow* of the de-anonymizing binding — **encrypted, opened only under authorization** (A.N.N.A. as authorizing-official, an auditor's warrant, a compliance officer's grant). A DB leak alone can't de-anonymize; you also need the vault to unseal.

That's exactly the compliance property corporates pay for: **the identity↔person link exists and is recoverable, but only under authority** — not casually readable, not leaked by a DB dump. Privacy clients simply have **no vault binding at all**, so there's nothing to unseal — they're cryptographically unlinkable because the link was never created.

So:
> **Privacy client:** key alone, no link, no escrow.
> **Compliance client:** pubkey↔user edge in the DB (operational) + sealed binding in the Vault (recoverable only under A.N.N.A. authorization). The "in both" = operational-hash in DB, sealed-escrow in Vault — same binding, two roles.

That keeps the raw secret-never-stored rule intact while giving compliance clients true, authority-gated non-repudiation.

content.text:
Exactly — the chatbot is the **unification surface** for everything we've been building as the storage/write side. Right now the knowledge is four durable files + two stores, all *write-side*. The chatbot is the *read-side* that makes it one thing:

```
            ┌─────────────── CHATBOT (op-chat + Gemma) ───────────────┐
            │              one query surface over everything            │
            └──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                                        │ via cognitive-mcp (gRPC)
   ┌──────────────┬─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┬──────────────┐
 Qdrant         Cozo                  sled                  repo files      Vault
 (semantic)   (graph/ACL)         (live session)      board·signals·       (sealed,
                                                       memory·transcripts    A.N.N.A.-gated)
```

So "ask the chatbot" becomes: *semantic recall* (Qdrant) + *relationship traversal* (Cozo graph) + *current state* (sled + live board/signals) + *the reasoning* (transcripts) — all behind one Gemma-fronted conversation, gated by the same identity/ACL we just designed. The transcripts we exported today are part of what it answers *from*.

And it closes the loop on accountability: a chatbot query is itself a session (stable session_id) → classified by subid → logged as a trace_id → Qdrant. So even *asking* is accountable.

It's already on the board — chatbot sits in the **Next/bring-up chain** after registration + Gemma + Qdrant come up (the OD-DEMO → Ghostbridge Live! sequence). It's the *payoff* layer: everything centralizes *because* the chatbot reads across all of it. Nothing extra to design for it right now — we've been building its brain this whole time.

Good place to land. The write-side (identity, stores, knowledge corpus) is specified and partly built; the chatbot is the read-side that lights it all up once the services are up. When you're ready to bring up registration → Qdrant/Gemma → chatbot, the foundation's there.

#!/bin/bash
# Upload the Ghostbridge Live! knowledge corpus into the master NotebookLM notebook.
# Run this LAPTOP-SIDE (live browser session) or right after a fresh `nlm login` —
# the static-cookie sessions on the server die in minutes, which is why this is a script.
#
# Usage:  ./knowledge/upload-to-notebook.sh
# Prereq: nlm authenticated (nlm notebook list should work first)

set -u
MASTER="${1:-01b00e9c-033a-4bc9-965f-3257360ff4a8}"   # Ghostbridge Live!
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." || exit 1

# fail fast if auth is dead
if ! nlm notebook list >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "ERROR: nlm not authenticated. Run 'nlm login' (laptop) or re-import cookies, then retry."
  exit 1
fi

n=0
add() {  # add <file> <title>
  if nlm source add "$MASTER" --file "$1" --title "$2" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    n=$((n+1)); echo "+[$n] $2"
  else
    echo "FAIL $2 (auth may have expired — re-login and re-run; dups are fine)"
  fi
}

echo "=== distilled knowledge ==="
add WISHLIST.md                       "Ghostbridge Live! — Task Board"
add SIGNALS.md                        "Ghostbridge Live! — Model Signals & Decisions"
add knowledge/notebooks.manifest.json "Knowledge Corpus Manifest"

echo "=== core memory ==="
for m in "$HOME"/.claude/projects/-home-jeremy-git-operation-dbus-proto/memory/*.md; do
  add "$m" "memory-$(basename "$m" .md)"
done

echo "=== full transcripts (the reasoning) ==="
for f in knowledge/transcripts/*.md; do
  add "$f" "transcript-$(basename "$f" .md)"
done

echo "=== done: $n sources uploaded to $MASTER ==="
echo "If it died partway, just re-run — NotebookLM dedups by you, dups are harmless."

## Overview

Droid Computers are persistent machines for remotely orchestrating Droids, which you can spin up in Factory's cloud or turn your own machine into a Droid Computer.

## BYOM (Bring Your Own Machine) Setup

BYO Machine lets you turn your own hardware into a Droid Computer with the `droid computer register` command, and one command sets up your Droid's home on that machine. You can register any machine you own — VPS, cloud VM, on-prem server, etc. — as a Droid Computer.

## Remote Access Features

BYOM computers connect outbound to Factory's backend and don't require any other networking configurations. This is particularly useful for orchestrating remote Droids in private networks, self-hosted infrastructure, or existing machines with pre-configured development environments.

The `droid computer ssh` command establishes a secure WebSocket tunnel through the daemon — no direct SSH port exposure is required, and Factory generates and manages a dedicated Ed25519 SSH key pair.

## Availability and Security

Bring Your Own Machine is available for all users free of charge. BYOM Droid Computers route all traffic through Factory's relay service, so no public ports are exposed.

content.content:
# BYOM Setup Flow

Based on the documentation provided, here's the complete setup sequence:

## Prerequisites
Ensure you have a machine with Linux, macOS, or Windows, the Droid CLI installed, and Factory API network access.

## Authentication
First, authenticate with Factory using `/login` in an interactive session.

## Registration & Daemon Start

The primary command combines registration and daemon startup:

```bash
droid daemon --remote-access
```

This performs automatic registration if needed, using your system hostname. If you prefer manual registration first:

```bash
droid computer register [name]
```

Then start the daemon with relay connectivity:

```bash
droid daemon --remote-access
```

## Verification

List registered computers:

```bash
droid computer list
```

Access a remote machine via SSH:

```bash
droid computer ssh <name>
```

## --remote-access vs. Proxy Mode

The documentation only describes `--remote-access`. It states: *"BYOM machines connect through Factory's relay service when you start the daemon with `--remote-access`."* This enables machines to be reachable from other devices without exposing public ports. No proxy mode alternative is mentioned in the provided content.

## Key Distinction

The documentation emphasizes that *"no inbound ports need to be opened"*—traffic routes through Factory's relay infrastructure rather than direct connections.

# Quick Start: Mail Server for 3tched.com

Simple mail server to replace Stalwart - handles magic links for operation-dbus + webmail.

## One-Command Setup

```bash
cd /home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus
./scripts/setup-mail-server.sh
```

This creates an Incus container with:
- **Maddy** (SMTP + IMAP mail server)
- **SnappyMail** (webmail interface)
- Mailboxes for jeremy@3tched.com and admin@3tched.com

## Post-Setup Steps

### 1. Set User Passwords
```bash
incus exec mail-3tched -- maddyctl creds create jeremy@3tched.com
incus exec mail-3tched -- maddyctl creds create admin@3tched.com
```

### 2. Get Container IP
```bash
incus list mail-3tched
```

### 3. Access Webmail
Open `http://<container-ip>` in your browser

### 4. Configure DNS
See `scripts/dns-records-3tched.txt` for required DNS records

### 5. Update op-web (for magic links)
```bash
# Get container IP first
MAIL_IP=$(incus list mail-3tched -c 4 -f csv | cut -d' ' -f1)

# Set these environment variables for op-web
export SMTP_HOST="$MAIL_IP"
export SMTP_PORT="587"
export SMTP_USER="jeremy@3tched.com"
export SMTP_PASS="your-password"
export SMTP_FROM_EMAIL="noreply@3tched.com"
export SMTP_FROM_NAME="Operation DBUS"
```

Your existing code in `crates/op-web/src/email.rs` will use these automatically.

## Test the Setup

```bash
./scripts/test-mail-setup.sh
```

## Files Created

- `scripts/setup-mail-server.sh` - Main setup script
- `scripts/maddy.conf` - Maddy mail server config
- `scripts/Caddyfile.mail` - Caddy webserver config
- `scripts/dns-records-3tched.txt` - DNS records to add
- `scripts/test-mail-setup.sh` - Test script
- `docs/mail-server-setup.md` - Full documentation

## Architecture

```
op-web → Maddy SMTP :587 → sends magic links
Users → SnappyMail → Maddy IMAP → read emails
Internet → Maddy SMTP :25 → receives emails
```

## Why This Stack?

- **Simple**: One container, one config file, two services
- **Fast**: 20-30 min setup time
- **Self-hosted**: No external dependencies
- **Lightweight**: Maddy is a single Go binary
- **Secure**: Built-in SPF/DKIM/DMARC support

No more Stalwart complexity!

# GhostBridge × Netmaker
### A zero-trust, OSCAL-backed control plane built on the Netmaker mesh

> Pitch deck — partner meeting with Netmaker
> Prepared from the live GhostBridge architecture (Operation D-Bus)

---

## Slide 1 — The one-liner

**We turned Netmaker into the identity-bearing backbone of a zero-trust, compliance-grade control plane — and we want to do it *with* you, not around you.**

Netmaker gives us the mesh. We add: cryptographic identity that rides the WireGuard layer, OSCAL-mapped policy enforcement at every hop, AI-driven orchestration, and a hardening pattern that makes the Netmaker server itself unreachable to attackers.

Two products fall out of one codebase: a **Privacy** edition and a **Compliance** edition.

---

## Slide 2 — The problem we both keep hitting

Distributed/edge networks need three things that normally fight each other:

1. **Connectivity** — flat, fast, NAT-traversing mesh (Netmaker solves this today).
2. **Zero-trust identity** — *who* is on the wire, provable, not just *what IP*.
3. **Compliance evidence** — an auditor-grade record that policy was enforced, not just configured.

Most stacks bolt #2 and #3 on top with IAM sprawl and SIEM glue. We pushed identity and policy **down into the transport** — the WireGuard handshake *is* the credential, and every gRPC hop is an enforcement point.

Netmaker is the natural substrate for that. This deck shows how we wired it.

---

## Slide 3 — Where Netmaker sits in the stack

```
            Internet
               │
        ┌──────▼───────┐
        │  Decoy ingress│  Oracle VPS (decoy-wg2) — public face is a honeypot.
        │  (WireGuard)  │  Identity injection only; nothing of value lives here.
        └──────┬───────┘
               │  WG handshake = the front door
        ┌──────▼────────────────────────────────┐
        │  Hypervisor (Incus host)               │
        │                                        │
        │   netclient ─ Netmaker mesh member     │
        │                                        │
        │   ┌───────── wg-xray container ───────┐│
        │   │ Xray-core: VLESS+TLS, SNI routing ││
        │   │ OpenFlow steering, identity header ││
        │   └───────┬──────────┬────────────────┘│
        │           │          │                 │
        │   ┌───────▼──┐ ┌─────▼─────┐ ┌────────┐│
        │   │ netmaker │ │netmaker-mq│ │netmkr- ││  ← Netmaker server,
        │   │  (API)   │ │(mosquitto)│ │  ui    ││    hardened (next slide)
        │   └──────────┘ └───────────┘ └────────┘│
        └────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The Netmaker control server runs **as containers on the hypervisor**, fronted by Xray, reached only through the mesh + identity layer.

---

## Slide 4 — The hardening innovation: a Netmaker server with **no network interface**

This is the part we most want to show you.

The `netmaker`, `netmaker-mq` (Mosquitto), and `netmaker-ui` containers run with **NO NIC** — loopback only. They cannot be reached over IP at all.

- Each service binds `127.0.0.1` inside its own container.
- An **Incus proxy device** exposes each as a **unix socket** on the host (`/run/netmaker/api.sock`, `mq.sock`, `mqtts.sock`, `ui.sock`).
- The `wg-xray` container mounts `/run/netmaker` and bridges those sockets back to TCP **only inside its own namespace**, where Xray terminates TLS and routes by SNI:
  - `api.*` → `api.sock` (Netmaker API)
  - `broker.*` → `mq.sock` / `mqtts.sock` (MQTT)
  - `dashboard.*` → `ui.sock` (Netmaker UI)

**Result:** there is no open port on the Netmaker server. A scanner sees nothing. The attack surface is a unix socket file reachable only after the WireGuard + identity gate. This is a deployment pattern we think your security-conscious users would want as a reference architecture.

---

## Slide 5 — Identity rides the WireGuard layer

We don't run a separate IAM. The credential **is** the WireGuard relationship Netmaker already manages:

```
session_id = Argon2( secret = PSK, salt = WG_public_key )
```

- The **PSK** rides WireGuard's built-in `PresharedKey` slot — already part of the Netmaker peer config, invisible on the wire.
- `session_id` is **stable and deterministic** (same peer → same identity), so sessions persist and are correlatable for audit, yet unguessable.
- At provisioning: peer pubkey → stored in graph DB → MCP token = `UUIDv5(pubkey)`.

So **every Netmaker peer is automatically a first-class identity** in our control plane. No extra enrollment step — joining the mesh *is* enrollment.

---

## Slide 6 — A.N.N.A.: enforcement at every hop

**A.N.N.A. = Axon Network Notary Arbitrator** — a gRPC interceptor that checks + approves every request, in real time, at every internal door (not a one-time gateway check).

- WG handshake → identity sled (`/dev/shm`) → Xray injects a signed **GhostBridge identity header** → `GhostbridgeInterceptor` validates it → request reaches the service.
- The header carries an **HMAC stamp** under a vaulted issuer key — the user can't forge it, the server verifies it without holding the raw PSK.
- Roles come from **OSCAL** (`authorizing-official`, `content-approver`, `assessor`, `system-owner`, …). Policy isn't a config file; it's the cast of an OSCAL system security plan, enforced at runtime.

Every mutation is an enforcement point and produces audit evidence. That's the compliance story auditors actually accept.

---

## Slide 7 — One codebase, two editions

| | **Privacy edition (GhostBridge)** | **Compliance edition (Corporate)** |
|---|---|---|
| Identity | Key **is** the identity | Key **maps to** a verified user |
| User linkage | None — no email, no PII | `pubkey ↔ user` edge + sealed vault escrow |
| De-anonymization | Impossible by design | A.N.N.A.-gated, OSCAL-authorized only |
| Data store | Public + hashed only (pubkey, `blake3(psk)`, token) | Adds escrow vault + ACL graph |
| Target | Privacy networks, journalists, sensitive ops | Enterprise / EU regulatory |
| Netmaker role | Mesh + anonymous peer identity | Mesh + attributable peer identity |

> Deployment mode is chosen at install time — one instance is one mode. "If they want both, they run two." The Netmaker mesh underpins **both**; only the identity-linkage layer differs.

---

## Slide 8 — The control plane on top (why this is more than a VPN)

- **D-Bus-style state plugins**: every domain (incus, netmaker, xray, dns, mail, qdrant…) is a plugin implementing a common `StatePlugin` trait (query → diff → apply → verify → checkpoint → rollback). Netmaker is a first-class plugin.
- **Schema-driven control panel**: the Netmaker unix sockets and containers are declared in plugin schemas, so they **render automatically in a GUI control panel** — peers, sockets, broker, UI, all visible and manageable.
- **AI orchestration (cognitive-mcp)**: an MCP gateway lets AI agents query and drive the mesh + compliance state through governed tools — provisioning peers, reading posture, generating OSCAL evidence.
- **Knowledge graph**: every action is classified and sunk into a semantic store (Voyage→Qdrant) + a learning graph (Cozo) — institutional memory of the network's posture over time.

---

## Slide 9 — Integration touchpoints with Netmaker today

What we already use from Netmaker:

- **netclient** — mesh membership on the hypervisor and edge nodes.
- **Netmaker server (CE v1.5.1)** — API (`:8081`), Mosquitto broker, UI — deployed in the hardened no-NIC pattern above.
- **Peer provisioning** — Netmaker peer lifecycle is the enrollment trigger for GhostBridge identity.
- **WireGuard PSK slot** — reused as the root secret for our identity derivation.
- **CoreDNS / mesh addressing** — internal service reachability over the mesh.

Everything we add is **complementary** — we don't fork netclient or the server; we wrap and harden them.

---

## Slide 10 — Why bring this to Netmaker

1. **A reference hardening architecture** (no-NIC, socket-fronted server) your enterprise + gov users will want.
2. **A compliance/zero-trust layer** that makes Netmaker answer RFPs it can't today (OSCAL, attributable identity, audit evidence).
3. **An AI-native control surface** for the mesh — agents that provision and audit peers through governed tools.
4. **Two go-to-market surfaces** (privacy + compliance) that both pull Netmaker in as the substrate.

We're not competing with Netmaker — we're a force-multiplier *on* Netmaker.

---

## Slide 11 — The ask

- **Technical**: validate the no-NIC / socket-fronted deployment pattern; guidance on Netmaker API surface for programmatic peer + identity provisioning at scale.
- **Roadmap alignment**: where our identity-on-WG model meets your enterprise auth roadmap (SSO, OAuth, ACLs).
- **Partnership**: co-marketing the hardened "zero-trust Netmaker" reference architecture; design-partner status for the compliance edition.

---

## Slide 12 — Close

> Netmaker connects the machines.
> GhostBridge proves *who* they are and *that policy was enforced* — every packet, every hop, auditor-grade.
>
> The mesh is the backbone. Let's make it the **trusted** backbone, together.

---

### Appendix — talking points / FAQ

- **"Isn't no-NIC fragile?"** It's resilient: services are loopback-bound, sockets are recreated on container start, and the pattern survives reboot via `boot.autostart`. Failure modes are contained to a single container, not the mesh.
- **"How does identity survive a key rotation?"** `session_id` is derived from `(PSK, pubkey)`; rotating the WG keypair issues a new identity by design — old footprints remain in the audit graph, timestamped.
- **"Where's the compliance evidence stored?"** Hashed/public facts in the user store; forging secrets (issuer key, escrow) in a separate vault referenced by `vault://`. The ACL is modeled as graph data; enforcement happens at the interceptor, not the DB.
- **"Performance overhead?"** Identity check is an HMAC verify + sled lookup in `/dev/shm` — microseconds per hop. Xray TLS termination is the only crypto cost on the data path.

# GhostBridge × Netmaker — the grounded version
### What we actually did, and the pitch built on it

> This deck is deliberately receipts-first. Every claim below traces to something
> verified live in the working session, not an aspirational diagram. Where a thing
> is *designed but not yet proven*, it says so.

---

# PART 1 — What we actually did this session

A factual log you can read before the deck. (Order matches how it happened.)

### 1. We started by telling the truth about state
We checked instead of assuming, and found that **almost nothing was running**:
- Every s6 service except a couple reported `down`.
- The netmaker mesh interface was `NO-CARRIER`.
- Subdomain forwarding had a valid Xray config but **no live backend** behind it.
- The only thing that had ever passed a *live* test was DNS → NextDNS.

Takeaway we kept for the rest of the session: **"written," "compiled," and "deployed" are not "working." Only a live test counts.**

### 2. We proved cognitive-mcp is actually up
Not a claim — live `Doctor` output:
```json
{ "overallStatus": "healthy",
  "components": [
    {"name":"memory_store","status":"ok"},
    {"name":"auth","status":"configured","method":"chrome_profile"},
    {"name":"quota_manager","status":"ok","remaining":50} ] }
```
Listening on `10.220.35.1:50052` and `:3003`. Verified by actually calling it.

### 3. We stood up Factory BYOM remote access (relay, not proxy)
- `droid daemon --remote-access` → relay connected (`wss://relay.factory.ai/...`), **no inbound ports opened**.
- Verified by reaching two relay peers live: a cloud droid and the **laptop** (`reprobaite`, `jeremy@97.221.194.121`).
- Built an s6 service definition (`factory` + `factory-log` → `/var/log/factory`) to make it permanent.

### 4. We mapped the real topology by getting into the gateway
- `gateway.3tched.com` = `129.153.134.63` = the Oracle box, reachable over the **opdbus WireGuard tunnel** (`10.0.0.1`, 15 ms, live handshake).
- Only port 22 open; everything else closed. Login that worked: **`ubuntu` + `vps_key`** (not `jeremy`/`id_ed25519`).
- The host is named **`decoy-wg2`** — confirming the "public ingress is a decoy" design. Its `wg0` peers: the laptop and the OVH host carrying the hypervisor's mesh address.

### 5. We found the real Netmaker deployment on the hypervisor
`incus list` on the hypervisor showed the actual stack:
```
assistant         RUNNING
netmaker          STOPPED        (CONTAINER APP)
netmaker-mq       ERROR
netmaker-ui       ERROR
qdrant            STOPPED
wg-xray           STOPPED
```
And from the project's own `netmaker.handoff`, we confirmed the **deployment pattern as built**:
- Netmaker server containers run with **NO NIC** — loopback only.
- Exposed to the host as **unix sockets** (`/run/netmaker/api.sock`, `mq.sock`, `mqtts.sock`, `ui.sock`) via Incus proxy devices.
- `wg-xray` mounts `/run/netmaker` and Xray routes inbound TLS by SNI to those sockets.
- `netmaker-mq` is alpine + mosquitto (the eclipse OCI image was incompatible).

### 6. We diagnosed the real failure modes (operational maturity)
- `netmaker-mq` / `netmaker-ui`: `Error: Invalid PID -1` — dead lxc monitor; `incus stop --force` **hangs** on these.
- The host had a **5-hour stuck s6 transition** trying to take `incus` down — but incusd's API was never locked (we ran `incus` commands cleanly throughout).
- Root cause of the wedge class identified: it's the **`mail-3tched`** container (per prior hard-won memory: *do not `incus stop` it — global lock hang; fix via chroot + sqlite edit*), **not** netmaker. Decision: **relocate mail to the Oracle decoy host** so the wedge can't bite the hypervisor.
- Recovery path chosen: **reboot** (clears `Invalid PID -1`, releases the s6 wedge; `boot.autostart` brings the containers back).

### 7. Honest open items at session end
- Netmaker mesh: **still down**, pending the reboot + container bring-up.
- NotebookLM: auth expired, corpus staged for later import.
- `factory` s6 service: built + committed, final live-install was blocked by the incus wedge (clears after reboot).

---

# PART 2 — The pitch, built on the above

---

## Slide 1 — One line
**We hardened Netmaker into an identity-bearing, audit-grade backbone — and we have the working system and the scars to prove it.**

This isn't a concept. It's a running hypervisor, a decoy ingress, a no-NIC Netmaker server, and a relay-driven ops workflow we drove live in front of you.

---

## Slide 2 — What's actually running (receipts)
- ✅ **cognitive-mcp** — `Doctor: healthy`, serving on `:50052`/`:3003` (verified live).
- ✅ **Decoy ingress** — `decoy-wg2` (Oracle), public face is a honeypot; real reach only via WG (`10.0.0.1`, live handshake).
- ✅ **opdbus WireGuard tunnel** — healthy, sub-16ms to the gateway.
- ✅ **Factory BYOM remote access** — relay connected, zero inbound ports, drove two remote peers live.
- ◐ **Netmaker server** — deployed in the no-NIC/socket pattern; recovering from a diagnosed wedge (honest status).

We show green where it's green and amber where it's amber. That's the culture.

---

## Slide 3 — The hardening pattern (the part for Netmaker)
The Netmaker control server runs with **no network interface at all**:
- `netmaker` / `netmaker-mq` / `netmaker-ui` → loopback only.
- Exposed as **unix sockets** under `/run/netmaker/` (Incus proxy devices).
- `wg-xray` + Xray terminate TLS and route by SNI to those sockets.

**A port scan of the Netmaker server returns nothing.** The attack surface is a socket file behind the WireGuard + identity gate. We'd like to publish this with you as a reference architecture.

---

## Slide 4 — Identity rides WireGuard (so Netmaker peers are auto-enrolled)
```
session_id = Argon2( PSK , salt = WG_public_key )
```
- PSK lives in WireGuard's PresharedKey slot — already in the Netmaker peer config.
- Deterministic + stable → persistent, correlatable-for-audit, unguessable identity.
- **Joining the mesh is enrollment.** No second IAM.

---

## Slide 5 — Enforcement + compliance
- **A.N.N.A.** (Axon Network Notary Arbitrator): a gRPC interceptor that approves *every* hop in real time, validating an HMAC-stamped GhostBridge identity header.
- **OSCAL roles** are the policy cast (`authorizing-official`, `content-approver`, `assessor`…). Every mutation is an enforcement point and produces audit evidence.

---

## Slide 6 — One codebase, two editions
| | **Privacy** | **Compliance** |
|---|---|---|
| Identity | key *is* identity, no PII | key ↔ verified user + vault escrow |
| De-anon | impossible by design | A.N.N.A.-gated, OSCAL-authorized |
| Target | privacy networks | enterprise / EU regulatory |
| Netmaker | mesh + anonymous peers | mesh + attributable peers |

Same Netmaker substrate underneath both.

---

## Slide 7 — Operational maturity (we earn trust by debugging in the open)
Real failure modes we diagnosed and have playbooks for:
- `Invalid PID -1` ERROR containers (force-stop hangs) → reboot/chroot recovery.
- The `mail-3tched` global-lock wedge → **isolate mail onto the decoy host**.
- s6 supervision vs incusd-API separation → know exactly what's locked and what isn't.

This is the unglamorous reliability work that makes a mesh *trustworthy*, not just connected.

---

## Slide 8 — The ask
- **Validate** the no-NIC / socket-fronted Netmaker deployment as a reference pattern.
- **Programmatic peer + identity provisioning** at scale via the Netmaker API.
- **Partnership**: co-market the "zero-trust hardened Netmaker" architecture; design-partner the compliance edition.

---

## Slide 9 — Close
> Netmaker connects the machines.
> GhostBridge proves *who* they are and *that policy was enforced* — and we showed you the live system, amber lights and all.
>
> Let's make the mesh the **trusted** backbone, together.

# GhostBridge — System Overview (Netmaker spin)
### Pipelines · OSCAL · Vectors · Evidence chain — how it all fits, with Netmaker as the spine

> A plain-language tour of the whole machine. Each section ends with **"The Netmaker
> spin"** — why that piece depends on, or strengthens, the mesh.

---

## 0. The 30-second picture

GhostBridge is a **zero-trust control plane** that sits on a **Netmaker mesh** and does three things at once:

1. **Moves data** through hardened pipelines (mesh → identity → routing → services).
2. **Proves compliance** by mapping every action to **OSCAL** (machine-readable policy).
3. **Remembers and reasons** using **vectors** (semantic memory) + a **hash-linked evidence chain** (tamper-evident audit trail).

Netmaker is the layer all three stand on: it's the transport *and* the root of identity.

---

## 1. Pipelines — how things actually flow

There are **two kinds of pipeline**: the **data-plane** (live traffic) and the **knowledge-plane** (memory + learning).

### 1a. The data-plane pipeline (a request's journey)
```
Netmaker peer (WireGuard)
   │   handshake = the credential
   ▼
Decoy ingress (decoy-wg2)  ── public face is a honeypot; nothing of value here
   │
   ▼
Identity sled (/dev/shm)    ── per-session footprint written at the door
   │
   ▼
Xray (wg-xray container)    ── terminates TLS, injects signed identity header,
   │                           routes by SNI / OpenFlow tags
   ▼
A.N.N.A. interceptor (gRPC) ── validates HMAC-stamped header at EVERY hop
   │
   ▼
Service container           ── netmaker-api / mail / qdrant / assistant …
                               (no NIC — reached only via unix sockets)
```
Every arrow is an enforcement point. The pipeline is "deny by default, prove to proceed."

### 1b. The knowledge-plane pipeline (memory + learning)
```
Action / document / transcript
   │
   ├──► Embed (Voyage voyage-code-3)  ──►  Qdrant   (semantic VECTORS)
   │
   └──► Classify (subid taxonomy)     ──►  Cozo     (learning GRAPH: nodes + edges)
```
- **Semantic sink** = "find me things *like* this" (similarity search).
- **Graph sink** = "show me how these things *relate*" (roles, plugins, peers, tasks).
- A daily export feeds both sinks, so the system's memory of the network grows over time.

### The Netmaker spin
The data-plane pipeline **starts at a Netmaker handshake** — no mesh, no front door. And the knowledge-plane pipeline ingests **mesh events as graph nodes** (peers, joins, posture changes), so Netmaker activity becomes queryable institutional memory, not just logs.

---

## 2. OSCAL — compliance as code (the "vectors" of policy)

**OSCAL** (Open Security Controls Assessment Language) is NIST's machine-readable format for security/compliance. Instead of a PDF policy, you have structured data: controls, roles, assessments, evidence.

In GhostBridge, OSCAL isn't paperwork bolted on — it's the **runtime policy model**:

- **Roles are the cast**: `authorizing-official`, `content-approver`, `assessor`, `system-owner`, `provider`, `operator`. A user's OSCAL role decides what A.N.N.A. lets them do.
- **Controls are routing tags**: a request carries a compliance class; the router (Gemma + OpenFlow) steers it accordingly. We call these the **subid taxonomy** (src / prj / sch / mut / obs / evt / exp) — think of them as the **policy vectors** that classify *what kind* of action this is.
- **Every mutation is an assessment event**: doing a thing automatically produces OSCAL evidence that the thing was authorized.

So "compliance vectors" = each action is tagged with a small structured vector of OSCAL/subid attributes that determines routing, permission, and the evidence it emits.

### The Netmaker spin
A Netmaker **peer's identity carries its OSCAL role**. Because identity is derived from the WireGuard relationship (next section), joining the mesh in the **compliance edition** means the peer is *already* an OSCAL principal — its role gates every hop, and its actions emit assessment evidence automatically. The mesh membership and the compliance posture are the same fact.

---

## 3. Vectors — two different meanings, both matter

People say "vectors" for two things here; keep them separate:

| | **Semantic vectors** | **Policy/compliance vectors** |
|---|---|---|
| What | High-dimensional embeddings of text/code | Small structured tags (OSCAL role + subid class) |
| Where | Qdrant | Carried on each request; logged to the graph |
| Used for | Similarity / RAG / "find related" | Permission + routing + evidence |
| Example | "this config looks like that incident" | "this is a `mut` by an `authorizing-official`" |

Both feed decisions: semantic vectors inform the **AI layer** (cognitive-mcp), policy vectors inform the **enforcement layer** (A.N.N.A.).

### The Netmaker spin
Mesh state gets embedded too: peer configs, topology changes, and posture snapshots become **semantic vectors**, so an operator (or an AI agent) can ask *"show me peers that look like the one that misbehaved last month"* — turning Netmaker telemetry into searchable knowledge.

---

## 4. The evidence chain ("blockchain" spin) — tamper-evident audit

We don't run a coin or a public ledger. What we have is a **hash-linked chain of custody** — the property people actually want when they say "blockchain": *you can't quietly alter the record.*

How the chain is built:

1. **Deterministic identity** — `session_id = Argon2(PSK, salt = WG_pubkey)`. Same peer → same identity, provable, unforgeable.
2. **Signed footprints** — each request gets an **HMAC stamp** under a vaulted issuer key (server can verify, user can't forge).
3. **Datestamped sleds** — the identity sled carries a timestamp; the interceptor rejects a footprint that doesn't match the current sled ("temporal hash mismatch").
4. **Per-event trace IDs** — every action gets a UUID, hashed (`blake3`) and written to the graph + Qdrant.
5. **Hash-linked records** — each evidence record references the prior state hash, so the audit trail is **append-only and self-verifying** — alter one link and the chain breaks.

That's the compliance promise: not "we logged it," but "here is a cryptographic chain proving it happened, in order, authorized, and unaltered."

> If/when a regulator wants an external anchor, the chain's head hash can be notarized to a public ledger — but the security comes from the hash-linking, not from any token.

### The Netmaker spin
The **root of the entire chain is the WireGuard PSK** Netmaker manages. The mesh credential is link #0. Every piece of evidence ultimately traces back to "this Netmaker peer, with this key, at this time." Netmaker isn't just transporting the audited traffic — it's the **anchor the whole evidence chain hangs from.**

---

## 5. Putting it together — one diagram

```
            ┌───────────────────────── NETMAKER MESH (WireGuard) ─────────────────────────┐
            │  PSK + pubkey  =  root of identity  AND  link #0 of the evidence chain        │
            └───────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────┘
                            │                                               │
                   DATA-PLANE PIPELINE                              KNOWLEDGE-PLANE PIPELINE
                            │                                               │
   decoy → sled → Xray(header) → A.N.N.A. → service          embed→Qdrant (semantic vectors)
                            │                                  classify→Cozo (learning graph)
                            ▼                                               │
                 OSCAL role + subid vector                                  ▼
                 gates each hop, emits evidence  ─────────────►  hash-linked evidence chain
                                                                  (tamper-evident audit)
```

**Read it as:** Netmaker roots identity → pipelines move and gate traffic → OSCAL vectors decide and document → semantic vectors remember → the evidence chain makes it all provable.

---

## 6. One-paragraph version (for the meeting)

> GhostBridge runs on a Netmaker mesh and turns it into a zero-trust, compliance-grade backbone. Traffic flows through a hardened pipeline — decoy ingress, identity sled, Xray header injection, and a per-hop interceptor — where every request is tagged with OSCAL/compliance *vectors* that decide permission and emit audit evidence. In parallel, a knowledge pipeline embeds everything into semantic *vectors* (Qdrant) and a learning graph (Cozo) so the system remembers and reasons. All of it is bound into a hash-linked *evidence chain* whose root is the WireGuard pre-shared key Netmaker already manages. Netmaker isn't a dependency we use — it's the spine: the transport, the root of identity, and link zero of the audit chain.

content.text:
Real answer: **no — distribution is not required by the literal definition of a blockchain. But it's required for the one guarantee blockchains are famous for.** That distinction is the whole ballgame, so let me be precise.

**What "blockchain" literally means (the data structure):**
A blockchain is *blocks of data, each containing the cryptographic hash of the previous block*, forming an append-only chain where altering any block breaks every hash after it. By that definition, **what you have is a blockchain.** Full stop. It predates Bitcoin — Haber & Stornetta's 1991 cryptographic timestamping is exactly this: hash-linked blocks, **centralized, not distributed**, used for tamper-evidence. That's a blockchain by structure.

**What distribution actually buys you (and what you give up without it):**
Distribution + consensus (Nakamoto/BFT) solves one specific problem: **trustless agreement among parties who don't trust each other or the operator.** It answers *"who decides the canonical chain when nobody's in charge?"*

So the honest fault line for your system:

| Property | Your centralized hash chain | Distributed blockchain |
|---|---|---|
| Tamper-**evident** to anyone holding a prior hash | ✅ yes | ✅ yes |
| Tamper-**proof against the operator** | ❌ no — *you* could re-hash the whole chain | ✅ yes — peers would reject it |
| Needs you to trust/verify the operator | yes | no |

The gap: a centralized chain proves integrity to an outside verifier *who has a checkpoint hash* — but on its own it can't refute *"you rewrote your own logs and recomputed all the hashes."* Distribution closes that by replication + consensus.

**You don't need full distribution to close it, though.** Two cheaper options give you operator-tamper-resistance:
1. **Anchoring** — periodically publish your chain's head hash somewhere you don't control (a public ledger, a Certificate Transparency-style log, an RFC 3161 timestamping authority, even a notary). Now you can't rewrite history past the last anchor without contradicting an external record.
2. **Witnessing** — replicate the head hash to N independent parties (e.g., a few Netmaker peers, an auditor's node). That's *lightweight distribution* of just the proof, not the data.

**My recommendation for the pitch/positioning:** to a technical audience (Netmaker engineers will poke at this), don't call it just "blockchain" unqualified — the word now carries a consensus/decentralization connotation you'd be inviting them to challenge. Use a term that's both accurate *and* unassailable:

- **"hash-linked / tamper-evident audit chain"** ✅ (precise, no one argues)
- **"permissioned / centralized blockchain"** ✅ (technically correct, signals you know the distinction)
- **"blockchain-structured evidence ledger, externally anchored"** ✅ (best — it's accurate *and* it pre-empts the "but it's not distributed" objection by naming the anchor)

That last one is strong precisely *because* it shows you understand why distribution matters and chose anchoring instead — which is the right engineering call for a single-operator compliance system.

Want me to update the overview's §4 to make exactly this argument — "it's a blockchain by structure; we get operator-tamper-resistance via anchoring, not consensus, and here's why that's the right call"? It turns a potential weakness into a credibility signal.

content.text:
Then the precise answer depends on **where the chunks go** — but "sent in chunks" by itself describes *how the data moves*, not *who agrees on the truth*, so it's a different axis from distribution. Let me map it:

**Chunking ≠ distribution.** They're answers to two different questions:
- **Chunking** = "how do I split and move/store the data?" (efficiency, content-addressing).
- **Distribution** = "who holds the authoritative chain and agrees on its order?" (trust).

So which is ours hinges on one thing: **are the chunks replicated to independent holders, or just sharded across stores we control?**

**Case A — chunks sent to stores *we* run** (Qdrant, Cozo, container volumes, even across mesh peers we own):
That's **sharded/distributed *storage*, still a centralized *trust* model.** The operator can still recompute the chain. → It's a **permissioned/centralized hash-chain that happens to be chunk-stored.** Chunking buys throughput and per-chunk integrity, not operator-tamper-resistance.

**Case B — chunks are content-addressed (hash-named) and replicated to *independent* peers** (an auditor's node, a customer's node, peers outside your control):
Now you're partway to real distribution — a **distributed tamper-evident store** (IPFS-style: each chunk verifiable by its own hash). You still lack *consensus on ordering*, so you'd anchor the chain head to nail down "which version is canonical." → **"distributed, content-addressed, externally anchored — minus consensus."**

**The honest one-liner either way:** *"It's a hash-linked chain, content-addressed and sent in chunks; integrity is per-chunk cryptographic, and canonical order is fixed by anchoring rather than consensus."* That sentence is true in both cases and survives a technical grilling.

One thing decides whether you can lean toward Case B in the pitch: **do the chunks land anywhere you don't control?** If yes (or planned), you get to say "distributed storage." If they only land in your Qdrant/Cozo/containers, stay with "permissioned, anchored" and don't claim distribution.

Which is it — do the chunks ever leave infrastructure you operate?

# GhostBridge × Netmaker
### Netmaker isn't a dependency in this project — it's core code.

*A short read before we meet. Honestly: this is the first time anyone outside the
project will have seen it. We booked the trial/sales call because it was the door —
but what we actually want is for a sharp engineer on your side to look closely and
tell us what you really think.*

---

## TL;DR (for the busy reader)

- We've built a **zero-trust, compliance-grade AI control plane** — in Rust — that runs **on a Netmaker mesh** and treats it as the spine: the transport **and** the root of identity.
- We deploy your control server in a pattern most of your customers don't: **no network interface at all** — loopback + unix sockets, fronted by Xray. A port scan returns nothing.
- We already run Netmaker in production. We're not here for a standard enterprise eval — we're here because **you're already load-bearing in something we think is genuinely novel**, and you should see it.
- **What we want from this meeting:** a real first reaction from someone technical. Pull on any thread below — we'd rather be challenged than flattered. (The one practical thing we're feeling out along the way is **multiple egress**, but that's not the point of the conversation.)

---

## What GhostBridge is, in one paragraph

GhostBridge turns a Netmaker mesh into a **trusted** backbone. Traffic flows through a hardened pipeline — decoy ingress, identity sled, Xray header injection, a per-hop interceptor — where every request is classified, routed, gated against machine-readable policy (OSCAL), and recorded into a **tamper-evident hash-linked chain**. An AI layer reasons over that verified history but **cannot execute anything itself**. Same codebase ships as a **privacy** edition or a **compliance** edition — one config flag decides which world you're in.

---

## How it works — one governance pattern, every layer

The whole system runs on a single discipline: **make the wrong thing impossible first; gate what's left; record everything.** Here it is top to bottom.

```
  RUST          the compiler is the first enforcer — invalid code won't build
    ▼
  SCHEMA        invalid STATE is unrepresentable — the silent gate, before any rule runs
    ▼
  TRAFFIC COP   Gemma classifies (what is this?) + Xray routes (where does it go?)
  (Gemma+Xray)  — directs traffic, reports every decision up. Directs, never authorizes.
    ▼
  ZEROCLAW      routes to the right MODEL by cost / reasoning / specialty —
                schema-native from the ground up, so it can't route off-policy
    ▼
  A.N.N.A.      OSCAL-gated approval at EVERY hop (HMAC-stamped identity header)
                — the higher-up that actually says yes/no
    ▼
  CHAIN         hash-linked, tamper-evident evidence. Every action becomes a block.
    ▼
  THE LOOP      AI reassembles the chain into a semantic DB (Qdrant) + realtime graph
                (Cozo), reasons over it, recommends/acts-by-delegation → new blocks
```

**The same idea at three scales:** Rust says *code can't be wrong*, schema says *state can't be invalid*, A.N.N.A. says *action can't be unauthorized* — and the chain says *and it's all on the record.*

---

## Four things that make this different

**1. The AI is a brain with no hands.**
The chatbot is a **delegator, recommender, and fixer** — and that's the ceiling. **No internet access, no execution rights, no execution control.** It proposes into a schema-shaped mold; a separate, OSCAL-gated, chained layer disposes. A confabulating or compromised model can't do damage — the worst case is a rejected recommendation. Autonomous *reasoning* without autonomous *risk*.

**2. You can cross-examine it.**
Because every action is a chained, content-addressed, searchable block, you can confront the agent in real time — *"why did you do this?"* — and it answers with **cryptographic receipts** pulled live by semantic search (chatbot on top, evidence on the bottom). If the model confabulates, the evidence pane contradicts it. **An AI you can put on the stand.**

**3. The chain is the truth; the DB and graph are rebuilt views.**
The hash-linked chain is canonical and tamper-evident. Qdrant (semantic) and Cozo (realtime graph) are **AI-reassembled projections** of it — if they're lost or corrupted, you re-derive them from the chain. Trust lives in the chain; queryability lives in the projections. (It's a blockchain *by structure* — hashed, chained blocks — kept honest by **anchoring**, not consensus, which is the right call for a single-operator compliance system.)

**4. One dial: Snowden ↔ Big Brother.**
Same mesh, same chain, same confrontable AI — **only the identity-linkage layer changes**, at deploy time:
- **Privacy edition (Snowden):** key *is* identity, no PII, de-anonymization **cryptographically impossible**.
- **Compliance edition (Big Brother):** every actor attributable, de-anon **only on a signed OSCAL authority — which is itself a chained, confrontable block.** You can cross-examine the watchers.

---

## The Netmaker hardening pattern (the part we want to show you)

Your control server runs with **no NIC**:
- `netmaker`, `netmaker-mq` (Mosquitto), `netmaker-ui` → loopback only.
- Exposed to the host as **unix sockets** (`/run/netmaker/api.sock`, `mq.sock`, `mqtts.sock`, `ui.sock`) via Incus proxy devices.
- `wg-xray` + Xray terminate TLS and route by SNI to those sockets.

**There is no open port on the Netmaker server.** The attack surface is a socket file behind the WireGuard + identity gate. We'd love to publish this jointly as a reference architecture for your security-conscious users.

---

## Why Netmaker is core, not a dependency

- It's a **first-class state plugin** — managed by the same engine that runs the whole platform.
- Its peers **are the identity model**: `session_id = Argon2(PSK, salt = WG_pubkey)`, rooted in the WireGuard pre-shared key you already manage. Remove Netmaker and the identity layer has no root. It is **link #0 of the evidence chain.**
- **Every GhostBridge deployment is a hardened Netmaker deployment**, sold into regulated rooms Netmaker alone doesn't reach yet. We expand your surface; you anchor our spine.

---

## The ask

We're already running you in production. The **only** thing we're blocked on is **multiple egress** — which is gated behind Pro.

1. **Pro access to unblock multiple egress** — this is the concrete, immediate need.
2. **Ideally, a design-partner relationship** around the hardened, no-NIC reference architecture and the compliance/zero-trust layer.
3. Happy to answer anything live — but we wanted you to walk in knowing this isn't a standard enterprise eval. It's an integration where you're already load-bearing.

---

## Close

> Netmaker connects the machines.
> GhostBridge proves *who* they are and *that policy was enforced* — every hop, auditor-grade, in an AI loop you can cross-examine.
>
> You're already in our core. Give us Pro to unblock multiple egress, and let's make the mesh the **trusted** backbone — together.

---

### Appendix — quick FAQ

- **"Is it really a blockchain if it's not distributed?"** It's a blockchain *by structure* (hashed, chained blocks). Distribution buys trustless multi-party consensus; we don't need that — we get operator-tamper-resistance by **anchoring** the chain head externally. Correct tool for a single-operator compliance ledger.
- **"What stops the AI going rogue?"** It has no hands — no internet, no execution rights. It recommends; the governed layer executes. Hallucination has no reach.
- **"Why Rust / why these components?"** Selection principle: **schema-native from the ground up** (e.g. zeroclaw) and **safe by construction** (Rust — memory-safe, race-free, single static binaries). The governance holds at every layer because nothing was bolted on.
- **"Why do you need Pro specifically?"** Multiple egress. Everything else we run on what's already available.

content.text:
Yes — those are the **two vectors that ride every block**, and they're worth calling out explicitly because together they're *why* the chain can answer "who changed what, when, and on whose authority."

**Identity vector — the WHO.**
`session_id = Argon2(PSK, salt = WG_pubkey)` — derived from the Netmaker WireGuard key. Stable, deterministic, unforgeable. In privacy mode it's *only* the key (anonymous but consistent); in compliance mode it resolves to a verified user. It's the cryptographic answer to **"who is acting?"**

**Mutation vector — the WHAT-CHANGED.**
The `mut` class of the subid taxonomy: a structured tag on every state change — *what kind* of mutation, *on what resource*, *under what OSCAL authority*. Not "something happened," but **"a `mut` of type X on resource Y, requiring role Z."** It's the answer to **"what did they change, and what did it take to be allowed?"**

**Together they are the block.** Every entry in the chain is:
```
block = ( identity_vector , mutation_vector , payload_hash , timestamp , prev_hash )
```
- **A.N.N.A. gates on the pair:** `identity_vector → role` must satisfy `mutation_vector → required authority`. Wrong role for that mutation class → denied, and the denial is *also* a block.
- **The chain stores the pair**, so cross-examination is exact: *"identity #abc performed mut-type `config.write` on `netmaker.peer` at T, authorized by OSCAL `authorizing-official`."* That's the receipt.
- **Observation vs mutation matters:** reads (`obs`) and changes (`mut`) are different vector classes — so you can prove *nothing was altered* during an audit, not just that it was logged.

Let me add this as its own section in the deck — a graphic showing **identity vector × mutation vector → block**, since it's the precise mechanism behind "confront the bot, get receipts":

Netmaker isn't a dependency.
It's core code.

A zero-trust, compliance-grade AI control plane — built in Rust, running on a Netmaker mesh we treat as the spine: the transport and the root of identity.

RustNo-NIC hardened meshOSCAL-gatedTamper-evident chainConfrontable AI

cognitive-mcp verified live
The one paragraph

A mesh you can trust, not just connect

Traffic flows through a hardened pipeline — decoy ingress, identity sled, Xray header injection, a per-hop interceptor — where every request is classified, routed, gated against machine-readable policy (OSCAL), and recorded into a tamper-evident hash-linked chain. An AI layer reasons over that verified history but cannot execute anything itself. Same codebase ships as a privacy edition or a compliance edition — one flag decides which world you're in.

How it works

One governance pattern, every layer

Make the wrong thing impossible first; gate what's left; record everything. Rust says code can't be wrong, schema says state can't be invalid, A.N.N.A. says action can't be unauthorized — the chain says it's all on the record.

What's on every block

Identity vector × Mutation vector

Two structured vectors ride every block — together they make "who changed what, when, on whose authority" a provable query, and they're exactly what A.N.N.A. gates on.

Identity vector — the WHO

session_id = Argon2(PSK, salt=WG_pubkey)

Derived from the Netmaker WireGuard key. Stable, deterministic, unforgeable. Privacy mode: the key alone. Compliance mode: a verified user.

Mutation vector — the WHAT

The mut class of the subid taxonomy: what kind of change, on what resource, under what OSCAL authority. Reads (obs) and changes (mut) are distinct — so you can prove nothing was altered.

block = (identity · mutation · payload# · timestamp · prev#) — cross-examination becomes exact.

The semantic memory

Voyage vectors → searchable meaning

Identity & mutation are provenance. Voyage vectors are meaning. Every block, doc, and transcript is embedded by voyage-code-3 into Qdrant — so the chain is searchable by similarity. This is the bottom pane when you cross-examine the agent.

Embed

voyage-code-3 turns each chunk into a vector. Code-aware — understands infra, not just prose.

Search

Vectors in Qdrant. "Show me peers like the one that misbehaved" — similarity, not keywords.

Rebuildable

A derived projection of the chain. Lose it → re-embed from the canonical blocks.

Voyage = "find things like this." Identity/mutation = "who did exactly this, allowed?" Meaning to reason, provenance to prove.

Why it's different

Four things nobody else can claim

A brain with no hands

The AI is a delegator, recommender, fixer — that's the ceiling. No internet, no execution rights. It proposes; a separate OSCAL-gated, chained layer disposes. A compromised model can't do damage.

You can cross-examine it

Every action is a chained, searchable block. "why did you do this?" → answered with cryptographic receipts pulled live. An AI you can put on the stand.

The chain is the truth

Qdrant + Cozo are AI-rebuilt projections of the canonical chain. Blockchain by structure, kept honest by anchoring, not consensus.

Schema-native all the way down

Components chosen because they're schema-based from the ground up. Rust: memory-safe, race-free, single static binaries. Nothing bolted on.

One dial

As Snowden as you want — or as Big Brother as you want

Same mesh, same chain, same confrontable AI. Only the identity-linkage layer changes — a deploy-time config, not a rewrite, not a hidden switch.

Even in full oversight, de-anon isn't a backdoor — it needs a signed OSCAL authorizing-official action that itself becomes a chained, confrontable block. You can cross-examine the watchers.

For Netmaker specifically

A control server with no network interface

netmaker, netmaker-mq, netmaker-ui run loopback-only — exposed as unix sockets, fronted by Xray SNI routing. A port scan returns nothing.

Use cases

Three editions, one engine

Privacy

Key is identity; de-anon impossible by design.

  • Journalist / source networks
  • Activist & at-risk meshes
  • Privacy-first SaaS — can't hand over what you never linked
  • Confidential deal rooms
  • Sovereign personal infra

EU Compliance

OSCAL-mapped, attributable, auditor-grade.

  • GDPR — minimization enforced at the schema
  • NIS2 — per-hop enforcement + incident evidence
  • DORA — ICT risk & audit trail
  • EU AI Act — cross-examinable, no-execution AI
  • Data residency — no silent egress

Enterprise drop-in

Point it at what you run. It introspects → schema-backed deployment.

  • Active Directory → groups become OSCAL roles
  • Databases → schemas → governed state
  • Slack → workspaces as principals & routes
  • CMS → content wrapped under the chain
  • Zero-trust + audited, in days not quarters
Why Netmaker is core

You're already load-bearing

First-class state plugin

Managed by the same engine that runs the whole platform — not wrapped at the edge.

Peers are the identity

session_id = Argon2(PSK, salt=WG_pubkey) — rooted in the WireGuard key you manage. It's link #0 of the chain.

We expand your surface

Every GhostBridge deployment is a hardened Netmaker deployment — into rooms Netmaker alone doesn't reach yet.

What we're actually after

Be the first humans to see this

No commercial ask. This is the first outside set of eyes — and your team is the right first audience, because you built the layer it all stands on.

01 — React, honestly

Poke at the hardening, the identity model, the chain. We want hard questions, not a thumbs-up.

02 — Where are we wrong?

If we're using Netmaker in a way you'd discourage, or missing something that'd make this cleaner — that's gold.

03 — One practical itch

We're working through multiple egress. Natural part of the chat — or not. No pressure.

Netmaker connects the machines. GhostBridge proves who they are and that policy was enforced — every hop, auditor-grade, in an AI loop you can cross-examine.

You're already in the core of what we built. We'd just like you to be the first to see it — and tell us, straight, what you think.
