toolUseResult.originalFile:
# GhostBridge × Netmaker
### Netmaker isn't a dependency in this project — it's core code.

*A short read before we meet. Honestly: this is the first time anyone outside the
project will have seen it. We booked the trial/sales call because it was the door —
but what we actually want is for a sharp engineer on your side to look closely and
tell us what you really think.*

---

## TL;DR (for the busy reader)

- We've built a **zero-trust, compliance-grade AI control plane** — in Rust — that runs **on a Netmaker mesh** and treats it as the spine: the transport **and** the root of identity.
- We deploy your control server in a pattern most of your customers don't: **no network interface at all** — loopback + unix sockets, fronted by Xray. A port scan returns nothing.
- We already run Netmaker in production. We're not here for a standard enterprise eval — we're here because **you're already load-bearing in something we think is genuinely novel**, and you should see it.
- **What we want from this meeting:** a real first reaction from someone technical. Pull on any thread below — we'd rather be challenged than flattered. (The one practical thing we're feeling out along the way is **multiple egress**, but that's not the point of the conversation.)

---

## What GhostBridge is, in one paragraph

GhostBridge turns a Netmaker mesh into a **trusted** backbone. Traffic flows through a hardened pipeline — decoy ingress, identity sled, Xray header injection, a per-hop interceptor — where every request is classified, routed, gated against machine-readable policy (OSCAL), and recorded into a **tamper-evident hash-linked chain**. An AI layer reasons over that verified history but **cannot execute anything itself**. Same codebase ships as a **privacy** edition or a **compliance** edition — one config flag decides which world you're in.

---

## How it works — one governance pattern, every layer

The whole system runs on a single discipline: **make the wrong thing impossible first; gate what's left; record everything.** Here it is top to bottom.

```
  RUST          the compiler is the first enforcer — invalid code won't build
    ▼
  SCHEMA        invalid STATE is unrepresentable — the silent gate, before any rule runs
    ▼
  TRAFFIC COP   Gemma classifies (what is this?) + Xray routes (where does it go?)
  (Gemma+Xray)  — directs traffic, reports every decision up. Directs, never authorizes.
    ▼
  ZEROCLAW      routes to the right MODEL by cost / reasoning / specialty —
                schema-native from the ground up, so it can't route off-policy
    ▼
  A.N.N.A.      OSCAL-gated approval at EVERY hop (HMAC-stamped identity header)
                — the higher-up that actually says yes/no
    ▼
  CHAIN         hash-linked, tamper-evident evidence. Every action becomes a block.
    ▼
  THE LOOP      AI reassembles the chain into a semantic DB (Qdrant) + realtime graph
                (Cozo), reasons over it, recommends/acts-by-delegation → new blocks
```

**The same idea at three scales:** Rust says *code can't be wrong*, schema says *state can't be invalid*, A.N.N.A. says *action can't be unauthorized* — and the chain says *and it's all on the record.*

---

## Four things that make this different

**1. The AI is a brain with no hands.**
The chatbot is a **delegator, recommender, and fixer** — and that's the ceiling. **No internet access, no execution rights, no execution control.** It proposes into a schema-shaped mold; a separate, OSCAL-gated, chained layer disposes. A confabulating or compromised model can't do damage — the worst case is a rejected recommendation. Autonomous *reasoning* without autonomous *risk*.

**2. You can cross-examine it.**
Because every action is a chained, content-addressed, searchable block, you can confront the agent in real time — *"why did you do this?"* — and it answers with **cryptographic receipts** pulled live by semantic search (chatbot on top, evidence on the bottom). If the model confabulates, the evidence pane contradicts it. **An AI you can put on the stand.**

**3. The chain is the truth; the DB and graph are rebuilt views.**
The hash-linked chain is canonical and tamper-evident. Qdrant (semantic) and Cozo (realtime graph) are **AI-reassembled projections** of it — if they're lost or corrupted, you re-derive them from the chain. Trust lives in the chain; queryability lives in the projections. (It's a blockchain *by structure* — hashed, chained blocks — kept honest by **anchoring**, not consensus, which is the right call for a single-operator compliance system.)

**4. One dial: Snowden ↔ Big Brother.**
Same mesh, same chain, same confrontable AI — **only the identity-linkage layer changes**, at deploy time:
- **Privacy edition (Snowden):** key *is* identity, no PII, de-anonymization **cryptographically impossible**.
- **Compliance edition (Big Brother):** every actor attributable, de-anon **only on a signed OSCAL authority — which is itself a chained, confrontable block.** You can cross-examine the watchers.

---

## The Netmaker hardening pattern (the part we want to show you)

Your control server runs with **no NIC**:
- `netmaker`, `netmaker-mq` (Mosquitto), `netmaker-ui` → loopback only.
- Exposed to the host as **unix sockets** (`/run/netmaker/api.sock`, `mq.sock`, `mqtts.sock`, `ui.sock`) via Incus proxy devices.
- `wg-xray` + Xray terminate TLS and route by SNI to those sockets.

**There is no open port on the Netmaker server.** The attack surface is a socket file behind the WireGuard + identity gate. We'd love to publish this jointly as a reference architecture for your security-conscious users.

---

## Why Netmaker is core, not a dependency

- It's a **first-class state plugin** — managed by the same engine that runs the whole platform.
- Its peers **are the identity model**: `session_id = Argon2(PSK, salt = WG_pubkey)`, rooted in the WireGuard pre-shared key you already manage. Remove Netmaker and the identity layer has no root. It is **link #0 of the evidence chain.**
- **Every GhostBridge deployment is a hardened Netmaker deployment**, sold into regulated rooms Netmaker alone doesn't reach yet. We expand your surface; you anchor our spine.

---

## What we're actually after

Plainly: **we want a knowledgeable human to look closely and react.** This is the first outside set of eyes on the project, and your team is the right first audience — because you built the layer it all stands on.

So in the meeting:
1. **Tell us what you really think** — poke at the hardening pattern, the identity model, the chain, the brain-with-no-hands. We want the hard questions, not a thumbs-up.
2. **Tell us where we're wrong about Netmaker** — if we're using something in a way you'd discourage, or missing a capability that'd make this cleaner, that's gold.
3. **The one practical itch:** we're working through **multiple egress** — if that's a natural part of the conversation, great; if not, no pressure.

No commercial ask. Just: be the first humans to see this, and tell us if it's as interesting as we think it is.

---

## Close

> Netmaker connects the machines.
> GhostBridge proves *who* they are and *that policy was enforced* — every hop, auditor-grade, in an AI loop you can cross-examine.
>
> You're already in the core of what we built. We'd just like you to be the first to *see* it — and tell us, straight, what you think.

---

### Appendix — quick FAQ

- **"Is it really a blockchain if it's not distributed?"** It's a blockchain *by structure* (hashed, chained blocks). Distribution buys trustless multi-party consensus; we don't need that — we get operator-tamper-resistance by **anchoring** the chain head externally. Correct tool for a single-operator compliance ledger.
- **"What stops the AI going rogue?"** It has no hands — no internet, no execution rights. It recommends; the governed layer executes. Hallucination has no reach.
- **"Why Rust / why these components?"** Selection principle: **schema-native from the ground up** (e.g. zeroclaw) and **safe by construction** (Rust — memory-safe, race-free, single static binaries). The governance holds at every layer because nothing was bolted on.
- **"What do you actually want from us?"** An honest technical reaction — you're the first outside eyes on this. Multiple egress is the one practical thing we're working through, but the reason we're excited is that you built the layer this all stands on.

# GhostBridge × Netmaker
### Netmaker isn't a dependency in this project — it's core code.

*A short read before we meet. Honestly: this is the first time anyone outside the
project will have seen it. We booked the trial/sales call because it was the door —
but what we actually want is for a sharp engineer on your side to look closely and
tell us what you really think.*

---

## TL;DR (for the busy reader)

- We've built a **zero-trust, compliance-grade AI control plane** — in Rust — that runs **on a Netmaker mesh** and treats it as the spine: the transport **and** the root of identity.
- We deploy your control server in a pattern most of your customers don't: **no network interface at all** — loopback + unix sockets, fronted by Xray. A port scan returns nothing.
- We already run Netmaker in production. We're not here for a standard enterprise eval — we're here because **you're already load-bearing in something we think is genuinely novel**, and you should see it.
- **Why we're sending this:** not an ask. We already run this in production on what's available today — we just figured the people who built the layer it all stands on should be the first to see what got built on top of it.

---

## What GhostBridge is, in one paragraph

GhostBridge turns a Netmaker mesh into a **trusted** backbone. Traffic flows through a hardened pipeline — decoy ingress, identity sled, Xray header injection, a per-hop interceptor — where every request is classified, routed, gated against machine-readable policy (OSCAL), and recorded into a **tamper-evident hash-linked chain**. An AI layer reasons over that verified history but **cannot execute anything itself**. Same codebase ships as a **privacy** edition or a **compliance** edition — one config flag decides which world you're in.

---

## How it works — one governance pattern, every layer

The whole system runs on a single discipline: **make the wrong thing impossible first; gate what's left; record everything.** Here it is top to bottom.

```
  RUST          the compiler is the first enforcer — invalid code won't build
    ▼
  SCHEMA        invalid STATE is unrepresentable — the silent gate, before any rule runs
    ▼
  TRAFFIC COP   Gemma classifies (what is this?) + Xray routes (where does it go?)
  (Gemma+Xray)  — directs traffic, reports every decision up. Directs, never authorizes.
    ▼
  ZEROCLAW      routes to the right MODEL by cost / reasoning / specialty —
                schema-native from the ground up, so it can't route off-policy
    ▼
  A.N.N.A.      OSCAL-gated approval at EVERY hop (HMAC-stamped identity header)
                — the higher-up that actually says yes/no
    ▼
  CHAIN         hash-linked, tamper-evident evidence. Every action becomes a block.
    ▼
  THE LOOP      AI reassembles the chain into a semantic DB (Qdrant) + realtime graph
                (Cozo), reasons over it, recommends/acts-by-delegation → new blocks
```

**The same idea at three scales:** Rust says *code can't be wrong*, schema says *state can't be invalid*, A.N.N.A. says *action can't be unauthorized* — and the chain says *and it's all on the record.*

---

## Four things that make this different

**1. The AI is a brain with no hands.**
The chatbot is a **delegator, recommender, and fixer** — and that's the ceiling. **No internet access, no execution rights, no execution control.** It proposes into a schema-shaped mold; a separate, OSCAL-gated, chained layer disposes. A confabulating or compromised model can't do damage — the worst case is a rejected recommendation. Autonomous *reasoning* without autonomous *risk*.

**2. You can cross-examine it.**
Because every action is a chained, content-addressed, searchable block, you can confront the agent in real time — *"why did you do this?"* — and it answers with **cryptographic receipts** pulled live by semantic search (chatbot on top, evidence on the bottom). If the model confabulates, the evidence pane contradicts it. **An AI you can put on the stand.**

**3. The chain is the truth; the DB and graph are rebuilt views.**
The hash-linked chain is canonical and tamper-evident. Qdrant (semantic) and Cozo (realtime graph) are **AI-reassembled projections** of it — if they're lost or corrupted, you re-derive them from the chain. Trust lives in the chain; queryability lives in the projections. (It's a blockchain *by structure* — hashed, chained blocks — kept honest by **anchoring**, not consensus, which is the right call for a single-operator compliance system.)

**4. One dial: Snowden ↔ Big Brother.**
Same mesh, same chain, same confrontable AI — **only the identity-linkage layer changes**, at deploy time:
- **Privacy edition (Snowden):** key *is* identity, no PII, de-anonymization **cryptographically impossible**.
- **Compliance edition (Big Brother):** every actor attributable, de-anon **only on a signed OSCAL authority — which is itself a chained, confrontable block.** You can cross-examine the watchers.

---

## The Netmaker hardening pattern (the part we want to show you)

Your control server runs with **no NIC**:
- `netmaker`, `netmaker-mq` (Mosquitto), `netmaker-ui` → loopback only.
- Exposed to the host as **unix sockets** (`/run/netmaker/api.sock`, `mq.sock`, `mqtts.sock`, `ui.sock`) via Incus proxy devices.
- `wg-xray` + Xray terminate TLS and route by SNI to those sockets.

**There is no open port on the Netmaker server.** The attack surface is a socket file behind the WireGuard + identity gate. We'd love to publish this jointly as a reference architecture for your security-conscious users.

---

## Why Netmaker is core, not a dependency

- It's a **first-class state plugin** — managed by the same engine that runs the whole platform.
- Its peers **are the identity model**: `session_id = Argon2(PSK, salt = WG_pubkey)`, rooted in the WireGuard pre-shared key you already manage. Remove Netmaker and the identity layer has no root. It is **link #0 of the evidence chain.**
- **Every GhostBridge deployment is a hardened Netmaker deployment**, sold into regulated rooms Netmaker alone doesn't reach yet. We expand your surface; you anchor our spine.

---

## What we're actually after

Plainly: **we want a knowledgeable human to look closely and react.** This is the first outside set of eyes on the project, and your team is the right first audience — because you built the layer it all stands on.

So in the meeting:
1. **Tell us what you really think** — poke at the hardening pattern, the identity model, the chain, the brain-with-no-hands. We want the hard questions, not a thumbs-up.
2. **Tell us where we're wrong about Netmaker** — if we're using something in a way you'd discourage, or missing a capability that'd make this cleaner, that's gold.
3. **The one practical itch:** we're working through **multiple egress** — if that's a natural part of the conversation, great; if not, no pressure.

No commercial ask. Just: be the first humans to see this, and tell us if it's as interesting as we think it is.

---

## Close

> Netmaker connects the machines.
> GhostBridge proves *who* they are and *that policy was enforced* — every hop, auditor-grade, in an AI loop you can cross-examine.
>
> You're already in the core of what we built. We'd just like you to be the first to *see* it — and tell us, straight, what you think.

---

### Appendix — quick FAQ

- **"Is it really a blockchain if it's not distributed?"** It's a blockchain *by structure* (hashed, chained blocks). Distribution buys trustless multi-party consensus; we don't need that — we get operator-tamper-resistance by **anchoring** the chain head externally. Correct tool for a single-operator compliance ledger.
- **"What stops the AI going rogue?"** It has no hands — no internet, no execution rights. It recommends; the governed layer executes. Hallucination has no reach.
- **"Why Rust / why these components?"** Selection principle: **schema-native from the ground up** (e.g. zeroclaw) and **safe by construction** (Rust — memory-safe, race-free, single static binaries). The governance holds at every layer because nothing was bolted on.
- **"What do you actually want from us?"** An honest technical reaction — you're the first outside eyes on this. Multiple egress is the one practical thing we're working through, but the reason we're excited is that you built the layer this all stands on.

The trust layer for sovereign AI.

Zero-trust, confidential, and auditable AI on accelerated infrastructure. Every action provable. Every model governed. Every decision you can cross-examine.

Confidential by construction Auditable — tamper-evident chain Sovereign — no silent egress Accelerated — GPU-native

Be the first to know when we open the doors.

3tched · sovereign AI control plane

# GhostBridge × Netmaker
### Netmaker isn't a dependency in this project — it's core code.

*A short read before we meet. Honestly: this is the first time anyone outside the
project will have seen it. We booked the trial/sales call because it was the door —
but what we actually want is for a sharp engineer on your side to look closely and
tell us what you really think.*

---

## TL;DR (for the busy reader)

- We've built a **zero-trust, compliance-grade AI control plane** — in Rust — that runs **on a Netmaker mesh** and treats it as the spine: the transport **and** the root of identity.
- We deploy your control server in a pattern most of your customers don't: **no network interface at all** — loopback + unix sockets, fronted by Xray. A port scan returns nothing.
- We already run Netmaker in production. We're not here for a standard enterprise eval — we're here because **you're already load-bearing in something we think is genuinely novel**, and you should see it.
- **Why we're sending this:** not an ask. We already run this in production on what's available today — we just figured the people who built the layer it all stands on should be the first to see what got built on top of it.

---

## What GhostBridge is, in one paragraph

GhostBridge turns a Netmaker mesh into a **trusted** backbone. Traffic flows through a hardened pipeline — decoy ingress, identity sled, Xray header injection, a per-hop interceptor — where every request is classified, routed, gated against machine-readable policy (OSCAL), and recorded into a **tamper-evident hash-linked chain**. An AI layer reasons over that verified history but **cannot execute anything itself**. Same codebase ships as a **privacy** edition or a **compliance** edition — one config flag decides which world you're in.

---

## How it works — one governance pattern, every layer

The whole system runs on a single discipline: **make the wrong thing impossible first; gate what's left; record everything.** Here it is top to bottom.

```
  RUST          the compiler is the first enforcer — invalid code won't build
    ▼
  SCHEMA        invalid STATE is unrepresentable — the silent gate, before any rule runs
    ▼
  TRAFFIC COP   Gemma classifies (what is this?) + Xray routes (where does it go?)
  (Gemma+Xray)  — directs traffic, reports every decision up. Directs, never authorizes.
    ▼
  ZEROCLAW      routes to the right MODEL by cost / reasoning / specialty —
                schema-native from the ground up, so it can't route off-policy
    ▼
  A.N.N.A.      OSCAL-gated approval at EVERY hop (HMAC-stamped identity header)
                — the higher-up that actually says yes/no
    ▼
  CHAIN         hash-linked, tamper-evident evidence. Every action becomes a block.
    ▼
  THE LOOP      AI reassembles the chain into a semantic DB (Qdrant) + realtime graph
                (Cozo), reasons over it, recommends/acts-by-delegation → new blocks
```

**The same idea at three scales:** Rust says *code can't be wrong*, schema says *state can't be invalid*, A.N.N.A. says *action can't be unauthorized* — and the chain says *and it's all on the record.*

---

## Four things that make this different

**1. The AI is a brain with no hands.**
The chatbot is a **delegator, recommender, and fixer** — and that's the ceiling. **No internet access, no execution rights, no execution control.** It proposes into a schema-shaped mold; a separate, OSCAL-gated, chained layer disposes. A confabulating or compromised model can't do damage — the worst case is a rejected recommendation. Autonomous *reasoning* without autonomous *risk*.

**2. You can cross-examine it.**
Because every action is a chained, content-addressed, searchable block, you can confront the agent in real time — *"why did you do this?"* — and it answers with **cryptographic receipts** pulled live by semantic search (chatbot on top, evidence on the bottom). If the model confabulates, the evidence pane contradicts it. **An AI you can put on the stand.**

**3. The chain is the truth; the DB and graph are rebuilt views.**
The hash-linked chain is canonical and tamper-evident. Qdrant (semantic) and Cozo (realtime graph) are **AI-reassembled projections** of it — if they're lost or corrupted, you re-derive them from the chain. Trust lives in the chain; queryability lives in the projections. (It's a blockchain *by structure* — hashed, chained blocks — kept honest by **anchoring**, not consensus, which is the right call for a single-operator compliance system.)

**4. One dial: Snowden ↔ Big Brother.**
Same mesh, same chain, same confrontable AI — **only the identity-linkage layer changes**, at deploy time:
- **Privacy edition (Snowden):** key *is* identity, no PII, de-anonymization **cryptographically impossible**.
- **Compliance edition (Big Brother):** every actor attributable, de-anon **only on a signed OSCAL authority — which is itself a chained, confrontable block.** You can cross-examine the watchers.

---

## The Netmaker hardening pattern (the part we want to show you)

Your control server runs with **no NIC**:
- `netmaker`, `netmaker-mq` (Mosquitto), `netmaker-ui` → loopback only.
- Exposed to the host as **unix sockets** (`/run/netmaker/api.sock`, `mq.sock`, `mqtts.sock`, `ui.sock`) via Incus proxy devices.
- `wg-xray` + Xray terminate TLS and route by SNI to those sockets.

**There is no open port on the Netmaker server.** The attack surface is a socket file behind the WireGuard + identity gate. We'd love to publish this jointly as a reference architecture for your security-conscious users.

---

## Why Netmaker is core, not a dependency

- It's a **first-class state plugin** — managed by the same engine that runs the whole platform.
- Its peers **are the identity model**: `session_id = Argon2(PSK, salt = WG_pubkey)`, rooted in the WireGuard pre-shared key you already manage. Remove Netmaker and the identity layer has no root. It is **link #0 of the evidence chain.**
- **Every GhostBridge deployment is a hardened Netmaker deployment**, sold into regulated rooms Netmaker alone doesn't reach yet. We expand your surface; you anchor our spine.

---

## What we're actually after

Plainly: **we want a knowledgeable human to look closely and react.** This is the first outside set of eyes on the project, and your team is the right first audience — because you built the layer it all stands on.

We're not asking for anything. We already run this in production on what's available today. We just figured the people who built the layer it all stands on should be the first to see what got built on top of it.

So in the meeting: if any of it is interesting, we'll happily go deeper. If not — no harm, no homework. Be the first humans to see this, and tell us if it's as interesting as we think it is.

---

## Close

> Netmaker connects the machines.
> GhostBridge proves *who* they are and *that policy was enforced* — every hop, auditor-grade, in an AI loop you can cross-examine.
>
> You're already in the core of what we built. We'd just like you to be the first to *see* it — and tell us, straight, what you think.

---

### Appendix — quick FAQ

- **"Is it really a blockchain if it's not distributed?"** It's a blockchain *by structure* (hashed, chained blocks). Distribution buys trustless multi-party consensus; we don't need that — we get operator-tamper-resistance by **anchoring** the chain head externally. Correct tool for a single-operator compliance ledger.
- **"What stops the AI going rogue?"** It has no hands — no internet, no execution rights. It recommends; the governed layer executes. Hallucination has no reach.
- **"Why Rust / why these components?"** Selection principle: **schema-native from the ground up** (e.g. zeroclaw) and **safe by construction** (Rust — memory-safe, race-free, single static binaries). The governance holds at every layer because nothing was bolted on.
- **"What do you actually want from us?"** Nothing, really — this is a heads-up, not a request. We already run it on what's available. We just wanted the people who built the layer it stands on to be the first to see it.

# GhostBridge — System Overview (Netmaker spin)
### Pipelines · OSCAL · Vectors · Evidence chain — how it all fits, with Netmaker as the spine

> A plain-language tour of the whole machine. Each section ends with **"The Netmaker
> spin"** — why that piece depends on, or strengthens, the mesh.

---

## 0. The 30-second picture

GhostBridge is a **zero-trust control plane** that sits on a **Netmaker mesh** and does three things at once:

1. **Moves data** through hardened pipelines (mesh → identity → routing → services).
2. **Proves compliance** by mapping every action to **OSCAL** (machine-readable policy).
3. **Remembers and reasons** using **vectors** (semantic memory) + a **hash-linked evidence chain** (tamper-evident audit trail).

Netmaker is the layer all three stand on: it's the transport *and* the root of identity.

---

## 1. Pipelines — how things actually flow

There are **two kinds of pipeline**: the **data-plane** (live traffic) and the **knowledge-plane** (memory + learning).

### 1a. The data-plane pipeline (a request's journey)
```
Netmaker peer (WireGuard)
   │   handshake = the credential
   ▼
Decoy ingress (decoy-wg2)  ── public face is a honeypot; nothing of value here
   │
   ▼
Identity sled (/dev/shm)    ── per-session footprint written at the door
   │
   ▼
Xray (wg-xray container)    ── terminates TLS, injects signed identity header,
   │                           routes by SNI / OpenFlow tags
   ▼
A.N.N.A. interceptor (gRPC) ── validates HMAC-stamped header at EVERY hop
   │
   ▼
Service container           ── netmaker-api / mail / qdrant / assistant …
                               (no NIC — reached only via unix sockets)
```
Every arrow is an enforcement point. The pipeline is "deny by default, prove to proceed."

### 1b. The knowledge-plane pipeline (memory + learning)
```
Action / document / transcript
   │
   ├──► Embed (Voyage voyage-code-3)  ──►  Qdrant   (semantic VECTORS)
   │
   └──► Classify (subid taxonomy)     ──►  Cozo     (learning GRAPH: nodes + edges)
```
- **Semantic sink** = "find me things *like* this" (similarity search).
- **Graph sink** = "show me how these things *relate*" (roles, plugins, peers, tasks).
- A daily export feeds both sinks, so the system's memory of the network grows over time.

### The Netmaker spin
The data-plane pipeline **starts at a Netmaker handshake** — no mesh, no front door. And the knowledge-plane pipeline ingests **mesh events as graph nodes** (peers, joins, posture changes), so Netmaker activity becomes queryable institutional memory, not just logs.

---

## 2. OSCAL — compliance as code (the "vectors" of policy)

**OSCAL** (Open Security Controls Assessment Language) is NIST's machine-readable format for security/compliance. Instead of a PDF policy, you have structured data: controls, roles, assessments, evidence.

In GhostBridge, OSCAL isn't paperwork bolted on — it's the **runtime policy model**:

- **Roles are the cast**: `authorizing-official`, `content-approver`, `assessor`, `system-owner`, `provider`, `operator`. A user's OSCAL role decides what A.N.N.A. lets them do.
- **Controls are routing tags**: a request carries a compliance class; the router (Gemma + OpenFlow) steers it accordingly. We call these the **subid taxonomy** (src / prj / sch / mut / obs / evt / exp) — think of them as the **policy vectors** that classify *what kind* of action this is.
- **Every mutation is an assessment event**: doing a thing automatically produces OSCAL evidence that the thing was authorized.

So "compliance vectors" = each action is tagged with a small structured vector of OSCAL/subid attributes that determines routing, permission, and the evidence it emits.

### The Netmaker spin
A Netmaker **peer's identity carries its OSCAL role**. Because identity is derived from the WireGuard relationship (next section), joining the mesh in the **compliance edition** means the peer is *already* an OSCAL principal — its role gates every hop, and its actions emit assessment evidence automatically. The mesh membership and the compliance posture are the same fact.

---

## 3. Vectors — two different meanings, both matter

People say "vectors" for two things here; keep them separate:

| | **Semantic vectors** | **Policy/compliance vectors** |
|---|---|---|
| What | High-dimensional embeddings of text/code | Small structured tags (OSCAL role + subid class) |
| Where | Qdrant | Carried on each request; logged to the graph |
| Used for | Similarity / RAG / "find related" | Permission + routing + evidence |
| Example | "this config looks like that incident" | "this is a `mut` by an `authorizing-official`" |

Both feed decisions: semantic vectors inform the **AI layer** (cognitive-mcp), policy vectors inform the **enforcement layer** (A.N.N.A.).

### The Netmaker spin
Mesh state gets embedded too: peer configs, topology changes, and posture snapshots become **semantic vectors**, so an operator (or an AI agent) can ask *"show me peers that look like the one that misbehaved last month"* — turning Netmaker telemetry into searchable knowledge.

---

## 4. The evidence chain ("blockchain" spin) — tamper-evident audit

We don't run a coin or a public ledger. What we have is a **hash-linked chain of custody** — the property people actually want when they say "blockchain": *you can't quietly alter the record.*

How the chain is built:

1. **Deterministic identity** — `session_id = Argon2(PSK, salt = WG_pubkey)`. Same peer → same identity, provable, unforgeable.
2. **Signed footprints** — each request gets an **HMAC stamp** under a vaulted issuer key (server can verify, user can't forge).
3. **Datestamped sleds** — the identity sled carries a timestamp; the interceptor rejects a footprint that doesn't match the current sled ("temporal hash mismatch").
4. **Per-event trace IDs** — every action gets a UUID, hashed (`blake3`) and written to the graph + Qdrant.
5. **Hash-linked records** — each evidence record references the prior state hash, so the audit trail is **append-only and self-verifying** — alter one link and the chain breaks.

That's the compliance promise: not "we logged it," but "here is a cryptographic chain proving it happened, in order, authorized, and unaltered."

> If/when a regulator wants an external anchor, the chain's head hash can be notarized to a public ledger — but the security comes from the hash-linking, not from any token.

### The Netmaker spin
The **root of the entire chain is the WireGuard PSK** Netmaker manages. The mesh credential is link #0. Every piece of evidence ultimately traces back to "this Netmaker peer, with this key, at this time." Netmaker isn't just transporting the audited traffic — it's the **anchor the whole evidence chain hangs from.**

---

## 5. Putting it together — one diagram

```
            ┌───────────────────────── NETMAKER MESH (WireGuard) ─────────────────────────┐
            │  PSK + pubkey  =  root of identity  AND  link #0 of the evidence chain        │
            └───────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────┘
                            │                                               │
                   DATA-PLANE PIPELINE                              KNOWLEDGE-PLANE PIPELINE
                            │                                               │
   decoy → sled → Xray(header) → A.N.N.A. → service          embed→Qdrant (semantic vectors)
                            │                                  classify→Cozo (learning graph)
                            ▼                                               │
                 OSCAL role + subid vector                                  ▼
                 gates each hop, emits evidence  ─────────────►  hash-linked evidence chain
                                                                  (tamper-evident audit)
```

**Read it as:** Netmaker roots identity → pipelines move and gate traffic → OSCAL vectors decide and document → semantic vectors remember → the evidence chain makes it all provable.

---

## 6. One-paragraph version (for the meeting)

> GhostBridge runs on a Netmaker mesh and turns it into a zero-trust, compliance-grade backbone. Traffic flows through a hardened pipeline — decoy ingress, identity sled, Xray header injection, and a per-hop interceptor — where every request is tagged with OSCAL/compliance *vectors* that decide permission and emit audit evidence. In parallel, a knowledge pipeline embeds everything into semantic *vectors* (Qdrant) and a learning graph (Cozo) so the system remembers and reasons. All of it is bound into a hash-linked *evidence chain* whose root is the WireGuard pre-shared key Netmaker already manages. Netmaker isn't a dependency we use — it's the spine: the transport, the root of identity, and link zero of the audit chain.

That's exactly the wedge a reboot clears — and now that `/run/netmaker` is persisted, they won't flap after reboot. input.content:
#!/bin/sh
# bringup-stack.sh — post-reboot bring-up of the GhostBridge/netmaker stack.
# Verified-correct order. Idempotent. Run after a reboot to bring everything up
# and set autostart so the NEXT reboot is hands-off.
#
# Root wedge fix already in place: /etc/tmpfiles.d/netmaker.conf recreates
# /run/netmaker on boot, so netmaker-mq/-ui no longer ERROR-flap.

set -e
echo "== 0. ensure socket dir exists (tmpfiles should have done this) =="
sudo mkdir -p /run/netmaker && sudo chmod 0755 /run/netmaker
ls -lad /run/netmaker

echo "== 1. wg-xray (network spine: 10.0.0.2 + 10.200.0.1) =="
sudo incus start wg-xray || true
sleep 4
sudo incus exec wg-xray -- ip -br addr 2>&1 | grep -E "10.0.0.2|10.200.0.1" || echo "  (check wg-xray ifaces)"

echo "== 2. netmaker-mq (mosquitto broker) =="
sudo incus start netmaker-mq || true
sleep 4

echo "== 3. netmaker (control plane, REST :8081) =="
sudo incus start netmaker || true
sleep 5
sudo incus exec netmaker -- ss -tlnp 2>&1 | grep 8081 || echo "  (8081 not yet listening — check 'incus info netmaker --show-log')"

echo "== 4. netmaker-ui =="
sudo incus start netmaker-ui || true
sleep 3

echo "== 5. egress so netmaker can reach the opdbus tunnel (10.0.0.x) =="
sudo iptables -C FORWARD -i netmaker -o opdbus -j ACCEPT 2>/dev/null || \
  sudo iptables -A FORWARD -i netmaker -o opdbus -j ACCEPT
sudo iptables -C FORWARD -i opdbus -o netmaker -m state --state RELATED,ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT 2>/dev/null || \
  sudo iptables -A FORWARD -i opdbus -o netmaker -m state --state RELATED,ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT

echo "== 6. set boot.autostart so the next reboot is hands-off =="
sudo incus config set wg-xray     boot.autostart=true boot.autostart.priority=100 || true
sudo incus config set netmaker-mq boot.autostart=true boot.autostart.priority=80  || true
sudo incus config set netmaker    boot.autostart=true boot.autostart.priority=60  || true
sudo incus config set netmaker-ui boot.autostart=true boot.autostart.priority=40  || true

echo "== STATE =="
sudo incus list --format csv -c ns4

# Incus Boot Wedge — Active Incident (2026-06-02)

## Symptom
System boots but does not get a full TTY. Currently accessible only via TTY 12 (degraded). s6 `incus` service is up (pid 603) but the boot sequence is wedged.

## Root Cause
`mail-3tched` Incus container is in ERROR state (`Invalid PID -1`). Its config has:
- `boot.autostart: "true"`
- `volatile.last_state.power: RUNNING`

On boot, Incus tries to restart it, fails with `Invalid PID -1`, and hangs/errors in a way that blocks clean TTY initialization.

## Why We Can't Fix Live
- `incus list` works from the degraded TTY (incusd is running, pid 603)
- BUT `incus stop --force` would acquire the Incus **global lock** and likely hang on the already-wedged container, making things worse

## Fix Plan — Live CD Chroot

### 1. Boot Artix live USB, mount root partition and chroot in

```bash
# example — adjust /dev/sdXN to actual root partition
mount /dev/sdXN /mnt
mount --bind /proc /mnt/proc
mount --bind /sys /mnt/sys
mount --bind /dev /mnt/dev
chroot /mnt
```

### 2. Edit Incus local sqlite DB directly

```bash
sqlite3 /var/lib/incus/database/local.db
```

Inside sqlite3, find and fix mail-3tched's config keys:

```sql
-- Check current state
SELECT * FROM instances WHERE name='mail-3tched';
SELECT * FROM instances_config WHERE instance_id=(SELECT id FROM instances WHERE name='mail-3tched');

-- Fix last_state.power so incus doesn't try to restart it
UPDATE instances_config 
  SET value='STOPPED' 
  WHERE key='volatile.last_state.power' 
  AND instance_id=(SELECT id FROM instances WHERE name='mail-3tched');

-- Disable autostart so it doesn't try again on next boot
UPDATE instances_config 
  SET value='false' 
  WHERE key='boot.autostart' 
  AND instance_id=(SELECT id FROM instances WHERE name='mail-3tched');

.quit
```

### 3. Exit chroot and reboot

```bash
exit
umount /mnt/dev /mnt/sys /mnt/proc
umount /mnt
reboot
```

## After Reboot
- Verify full TTY is restored
- `sudo incus list` — mail-3tched should show STOPPED and not ERROR

- mail-3tched has proxy devices for IMAP/IMAPS/SMTP pointing at unix sockets under `/run/mail-3tched/` — check those exist

# Incus Boot Wedge — GENERALIZED ROOT CAUSE (updated 2026-06-13)

## The real pattern (this is the recurring bug)
Any incus container whose **proxy devices bind host sockets under a `/run/<svc>/` dir**
will ERROR-wedge after a reboot, because `/run` is **tmpfs and the dir is wiped on boot**.
Sequence: dir gone → proxy device can't create its listen socket → container fails →
**ERROR `Invalid PID -1` → flaps RUNNING↔ERROR → holds incusd's global WRITE lock →
every `incus start` / `incus move` / `config set` hangs (exit 124).** Reads still work.

Seen on `mail-3tched` (2026-06-02, sockets under `/run/mail-3tched/`) and on
`netmaker-mq`/`netmaker-ui` (2026-06-13, sockets under `/run/netmaker/`). Same cause.

## THE FIX (durable, do this for every such container)
Create a tmpfiles.d rule so the dir is recreated on every boot:
```
# /etc/tmpfiles.d/netmaker.conf
d /run/netmaker 0755 root root -
```
Processed by the `tmpfiles-setup` s6 oneshot at boot. Applied for netmaker on 2026-06-13.
Do the same for any future container with `/run/<svc>/` proxy sockets.

## Rules
- **Never `incus stop --force` an ERROR container** — acquires the global lock and hangs harder.
- **Never blind-reboot before the tmpfiles fix is in place** — reboot re-wipes the dir and
  re-wedges identically. WITH the tmpfiles rule, reboot is the correct unblock (clears the
  wedged write-lock; containers come up clean).
- `mail-3tched` is **GONE from this host** (only an orphan btrfs subvol `containers/mail-3tched`
  remained as of 2026-06-13). See [[project-incus-storage-pool]] for the loop-pool issue that
  compounded the ERROR pressure.

content.text:
Good question — and it cuts right at tonight's wedge, since the broker *is* the problem container (`netmaker-mq`). Straight answer:

**xray — can *front* the broker, can't *be* it.**
xray is a transport router (VLESS/Reality/TLS, SNI/tag routing). MQTT is just TCP under the hood, so xray can terminate TLS, route `broker.ghostbridge.tech`, and forward to a broker — but it does **not speak MQTT** (no pub/sub, topics, retained messages, QoS). Something still has to actually *be* the broker.

**gemma — no.**
Gemma's an LLM for subid classification + tag routing. It's not a message broker in any sense. Not a candidate.

**But here's the win you're actually reaching for:** the broker doesn't need to be xray/gemma — and it doesn't need to be that **no-NIC `netmaker-mq` container** either. That container is the whole wedge: its proxy sockets under `/run/netmaker/` are what ERROR on boot. Kill the container, kill the wedge.

**Move the broker to the host.** Run mosquitto (or a Rust broker like `rumqttd`) as a **host s6 service** on `127.0.0.1:1883/8883`, and let xray front it for TLS/routing. Then:
- `netmaker` points `BROKER_ENDPOINT=mqtt://127.0.0.1:1883` (already does)
- **`netmaker-mq` container is deleted** → no `/run/netmaker/mq.sock` proxy device → the boot wedge that's eaten tonight **structurally cannot happen**
- one fewer no-NIC container to rebuild on the `array` pool

So: xray routes it, host runs it, gemma stays out of it. That's strictly better than what we had — it removes the exact thing that keeps wedging incusd.

content.text:
Yes to one, "sort of" to the other — and the distinction matters for your design:

**D-Bus brokers — yes, real and first-class.**
D-Bus *is* a message bus with a broker. The classic one is `dbus-daemon`; the modern high-performance one is **`dbus-broker`** (the systemd-team reimplementation). Pub/sub happens via **signals** (broadcast) + match rules. And you already run D-Bus heavily (the op-dbus projection plane). So for your system's *own* internal eventing, a D-Bus broker is native and already in the stack.

**gRPC "brokers" — not a built-in concept, but buildable.**
gRPC is RPC (unary + streaming), not a broker protocol. There's no MQTT-equivalent "gRPC broker" standard. But you can implement broker-style pub/sub **over gRPC bidi/server-streaming** — a service with `Subscribe`/`Publish` methods, fan-out on the server side. Your `op-grpc-bridge` is already gRPC, so a pub/sub service there is feasible. It's something you build, not something you drop in.

**The hard constraint that decides it: netmaker only speaks MQTT.**
netclients/netmaker connect to a broker via `mqtt://…` — MQTT on the wire (1883/8883), pub/sub, retained messages, QoS. It will **not** talk to a D-Bus broker or a gRPC pub/sub service. So you cannot swap mosquitto for either *for netmaker's use* without an MQTT-speaking shim in front. That's the wall.

So the clean split is **two buses for two consumers**:
- **MQTT (mosquitto, or Rust `rumqttd`)** — only because netmaker demands MQTT. Keep it minimal, run it **on the host** (s6), front it with xray. That alone deletes the wedging `netmaker-mq` container.
- **D-Bus / gRPC** — your system's *own* eventing and control plane. Native, already there, no mosquitto involved.

Don't try to make one bus serve both — netmaker's MQTT requirement is non-negotiable on its side; everything else is yours and should ride D-Bus/gRPC.

Net for the rebuild: we **don't rebuild `netmaker-mq` as a no-NIC container.** Broker → host (mosquitto or rumqttd) → fronted by xray. Want me to go that route when we get to the broker element?

content.text:
You're right to correct me — I overstated it. Let me be precise:

**On "netmaker only speaks MQTT" — you're correct, I was sloppy.**
Netmaker requires the **MQTT protocol**, but MQTT is an **open standard**, so the **broker implementation is fully swappable**. It is *not* tied to mosquitto. Any MQTT-compliant broker works:
- **`rumqttd`** (Rust, embeddable, host-native — fits your stack)
- EMQX, VerneMQ, NanoMQ, HiveMQ, etc.

So "replace the broker" is absolutely valid — swap mosquitto for a lighter/Rust one, run it on the host, done. The universality cuts *your* way. The only thing you can't do is make netmaker speak a **non-MQTT** bus (D-Bus/gRPC) without a protocol translator in front. So: replace the *implementation* freely; you just keep MQTT *on netmaker's wire*.

**On reflection — yes, it should be involved, but only on the gRPC leg.**
Reflection is a **gRPC** mechanism: a server advertises its services/methods so clients discover them dynamically (it's exactly what your tonic-web MCP shim relies on). It has **no equivalent in MQTT** (MQTT "discovery" is via topics).

So where reflection belongs:
- **If you build a gRPC pub/sub broker** (Subscribe/Publish over bidi streaming on `op-grpc-bridge`), then **yes — include reflection**, to match your stack standard (`tonic-web + reflection + accept_http1`, which you already standardized across op-grpc-bridge / op-cognitive-mcp / op-openvswitch-daemon / op-chat). A new broker service missing reflection *would* be the inconsistency — so good catch.
- **On the MQTT leg (netmaker's broker)** — reflection doesn't apply; nothing's missing there.

So the clean picture:
- **netmaker's broker** = any MQTT broker (swap mosquitto → `rumqttd` on host). MQTT wire, no reflection concept.
- **your internal eventing** = D-Bus signals and/or a gRPC pub/sub service **with reflection** — discoverable, consistent with the rest of the stack.

Two buses, two discovery models — and reflection is the right discovery model for the gRPC one. Want to go `rumqttd`-on-host for netmaker and fold the internal pub/sub into `op-grpc-bridge` with reflection?

In other words, it's part of your "wrap every sub-HTTP protocol as gRPC so xray can route it with identity" pattern — `rumqttc` is the client that talks MQTT on one side and feeds the gRPC bridge on the other.

So it's already *yours*, already proven to talk to the broker. Adding `rumqttd` (the broker sibling) is staying inside the exact same library family you're already running — which is a good consistency argument for it.

content.text:
You're right — I had the answer and kept digging. Here it is, straight:

**Yes. `rumqttd` does everything netmaker's broker needs.** From its own generated config:

- **Username/password auth** — `[v4.1.connections.auth]` with `user = "password"` pairs (config lines 48–51). That covers netmaker's `allow_anonymous false` + credentials.
- **TLS** — `[v4.x.tls]` with `capath`/`certpath`/`keypath` (lines 57–61), i.e. the `8883` mqtts listener.
- **Listeners** — per-port `listen = "..."`, so `127.0.0.1:1883` + `127.0.0.1:8883`.

So the functional answer to "can Rust do what netmaker wants" is **yes** — auth + TLS + loopback listeners, all there.

**One real difference** (not a blocker): mosquitto stores **hashed** passwords in a `password_file`; rumqttd puts the credential **inline (plaintext) in the TOML**. Same auth result for netmaker's single MQ user — just plaintext-in-config vs hashed-file. If that matters for your threat model, say so; otherwise it's fine for a loopback broker.

That's the answer. rumqttd is a go for the broker leg.

Right — and that's a fair hit. The watcher was my own scaffolding to know when an external `cargo` build finished; it's not going into your system. But the instinct behind it (poll/watch/wait) is exactly the pattern your architecture rejects, and I should be thinking in your model instead.

Your model, as I understand it: **write to `/dev/shm`, react** — not watch/poll/query/index. The authoritative state already lives in shm (`/dev/shm/live-schema.json`, the identity sled), so a component **reads the current shm state**, which is always true *now* — it never has to watch for changes or poll a socket. And xray **greets every incoming connection** rather than watching for them. State is pushed to shm once and is durable for the session; consumers read it, they don't subscribe-and-wait.

So nothing I build should introduce a watcher, a polling loop, an index-and-query, or a "wait for X." If something needs to know state, it reads shm. If something needs to act on arrival, the arrival itself triggers it (xray greeting), not a watcher.

Is that the principle you're holding me to — **shm is the single source of present-state, read it; don't watch/poll/query/index** — or is there a sharper edge to it I'm still missing?

name: project-shm-reactive-principle
description: Core architecture principle — /dev/shm is the single source of PRESENT state; components READ it. The system does NOT watch/poll/query/index/wait. Arrival triggers action (xray greets connections), not a watcher.
metadata:
  type: project
---

**This system does not watch, poll, query, index, or wait. It uses `/dev/shm`.**

`/dev/shm` holds the authoritative PRESENT state (`/dev/shm/live-schema.json`, the identity
sled, xray config). A component **reads current shm state** — which is always true *now* — it
never subscribes-and-waits or polls a socket. State is written once and is durable for the
whole session; consumers read it on demand.

Action is triggered by **arrival**, not by a watcher: **xray greets every incoming
connection** and acts; nothing sits in a loop watching for events.

**Why:** The user designed it this way deliberately and holds me to it. My instinct to build
watchers / `until` poll-loops / "wait for X" / index-then-query is the exact anti-pattern.
Confirmed verbatim: "this system doesn't wait, watch, query, index... we have shm" → "exactly".

**How to apply:**
- Never introduce a watcher, polling loop, `inotify`/`watch_*`, "wait for ready", or
  index-and-query into the system design. If something needs state, it READS shm.
- If something must act on an event, the event itself (e.g. xray greeting a connection) is the
  trigger — no separate watcher process.
- The identity sled is written at handshake/activity and read from shm; it is NOT refreshed by
  a watcher (see [[project-key-derivation]]). Relates to [[feedback-no-unfounded-generalizations]]
  (don't assume a watch/poll design without checking).
- (Scaffolding for MY external tooling — e.g. waiting on a `cargo` build — is not part of the
  system, but prefer reacting to completion notifications over poll-loops there too.)

Verified, not assumed — and this is a real finding: **netmaker currently has *no* device to reach the broker.** Its devices are only `api-sock` (exposes its 8081 *out* to the host), `incus-socket`, and the two btrfs disks (`nm-dnsconfig`, `nm-sqldata`). That almost certainly explains the MQ "token timeout" failures from the transcript — the no-NIC netmaker was dialing `127.0.0.1:1883` inside its own empty loopback, with nothing there.

The host-rumqttd approach actually **fixes** that cleanly with one proxy device (`bind: container`) mapping the container's loopback to the host broker:
```
type: proxy, bind: container
listen:  tcp:127.0.0.1:1883   # inside netmaker container
connect: tcp:127.0.0.1:1883   # host → host rumqttd
```

content.text:
Scoped answer, not a blanket one:

**Netmaker itself can't have reflection/tonic-web** — those are gRPC-*server* features, and netmaker is a REST/HTTP server (verified: it answered plain HTTP on :8081). It has no gRPC surface to reflect.

**But your instinct is right for the *plane* it sits on.** If you want netmaker on the internal gRPC plane consistently — the way you standardized `tonic-web + reflection + accept_http1` across `op-grpc-bridge`, `op-cognitive-mcp`, `op-openvswitch-daemon`, `op-chat` — then it needs a **gRPC adapter wrapping its REST**, with its **own proto + reflection + tonic-web**. Exactly the pattern `op-grpc-adapters/src/adapters/mq.rs` already uses for MQTT (`MqService`). So you'd add a `NetmakerService` proto/adapter alongside `MqService`. Netmaker stays REST; the adapter gives it the gRPC face + reflection.

**One address correction so the answer's precise:**
- **`10.0.0.1`** is the **gateway VPS / decoy-injection "parking lot"** (`10.0.0.0/24` = injection only, per your own definition) — traffic there is routed REST through xray; it doesn't need reflection.
- **`10.200.0.1`** is the **gRPC plane** (grpc-uplink) — *that's* where reflection/tonic-web matters.

So: if netmaker is to be consumed **as gRPC on `10.200.0.1`** (by browsers/MCP over gRPC-web through xray), then **yes — give it an adapter with its own proto + reflection + tonic-web.** If it's only serving **REST via the subdomain forwarder + MQTT to netclients**, it doesn't need it — xray just routes the REST.

Did you mean `10.200.0.1` (the gRPC plane)? If so, the adapter-with-reflection is the consistent move, and it's a small addition next to the existing `MqService`.

That's the learning moment in one screen. Look at what just happened: the second block was **reconstructed entirely from the running binary** — grpcurl never touched your `.proto` file, yet it printed your schema back. Here's the chain that makes it work:

**1. You write the proto** → `crates/op-grpc-adapters/proto/adapters.proto` (the `service MqService { ... }` you saw first).

**2. `build.rs` compiles it AND serializes the schema:**
```rust

    .file_descriptor_set_path(out.join("adapters_descriptor.bin"))  // ← schema-as-bytes
    .compile_protos(&["proto/adapters.proto"], &["proto"])?;
```
That `.bin` is a **FileDescriptorSet** — the entire proto (services, methods, messages, field numbers, types) encoded as protobuf *about* protobuf.

**3. `lib.rs` bakes those bytes into the program:**
```rust
pub const FILE_DESCRIPTOR_SET: &[u8] =
    tonic::include_file_descriptor_set!("adapters_descriptor");
```

**4. `server.rs` hands them to the reflection service:**
```rust
let reflection = ReflectionBuilder::configure()
    .register_encoded_file_descriptor_set(FILE_DESCRIPTOR_SET)
    .build_v1()?;
... .add_service(reflection)
```

Right — a single-file mount is the trap: the writer (`schema_bridge.rs`) writes the sled via **atomic rename** (`fs::rename(tmp, SHM_SLED_PATH)`), which swaps in a *new inode*. A single-file bind mount is pinned to the **old inode**, so after the next sled write the container silently reads a dead/stale copy — exactly the "sled disappears/desyncs" you've been hit by. The hashes match *right now* but it'd desync on the next write. That's the copy behavior you're warning about.

The fix that's a **live view, not a copy**: mount the `/dev/shm` **directory**, so the container always resolves `plugin_schema.dat` by name and gets the current inode after any rename.

Two notes to be straight about the qdrant part: the **unfiltered** scroll proved retrieval (839,923 real repomix chunks). The **text-filter** query I just tried errored (that JSON traceback) — because `content` has no full-text index configured in this collection, so qdrant rejected the `match.text` filter. And true *semantic* search needs a query *embedding* (voyage-code-3, 1024-dim) — which needs the embedder online. So: data's all there and retrievable; meaning-search needs the embed path. Not a claim beyond what I showed.

On **cozo** (since you said you're unsure) — and you confirmed my read:

**Cozo is your graph/relational store; qdrant is your vector store. Two sinks, two jobs.**
- `cognitive.db` is a **directory** because CozoDB is **embedded** (RocksDB-backed) — not a server you connect to over a port. `server.rs` says it plainly: *"Single persistent backend (CozoDB) hosts every relation."* One db, every relation (memory, sessions, graph edges).
- **How you query it: CozoScript — a Datalog dialect.** Instead of SQL joins, you write rules like `?[entity, related] := *edges[entity, _, related]` and it walks relationships transitively. That's what makes it a *graph*: it's built to answer "how does X connect to Y, N hops out" cheaply — the thing qdrant's vector similarity *can't* do.
- **The split in your architecture:** qdrant = "find me things *like* this" (semantic vectors). cozo = "show me how these things *relate*" (the learning graph — nodes + edges). Same knowledge, two access patterns.
- **Because it's embedded (single-writer lock), you don't query cozo directly** — you go *through* cognitive-mcp, which owns the open handle. That's why the db dir is held by the `op-cognitive-mcp` process.

So the full picture is now live and proven: **cognitive-mcp up → queries work → qdrant (839k vectors) queryable → cozo (graph relations) is its backend.** Want me to run a cozo-backed query *through* cognitive-mcp to show the graph side answering, the same way I showed the notebook/qdrant side?

- The tree projects the MCP at `org.opdbus.CognitiveMcp` → `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/cognitive_mcp` (`org.opdbus.CognitiveMcpV1`) with the generic surface: `ListTools()`, `GetToolSchema(name)`, `CallTool(name, args_json)` — `crates/op-cognitive-mcp/src/dbus_interface.rs`.
- cognitive-mcp already serves gRPC (`CognitiveToolService`, port 50052, bound to the WG interface IP) alongside HTTP/SSE on 3003 — `crates/op-cognitive-mcp/src/main.rs`. The transports are independently toggleable via the `cognitive_mcp` state plugin (`http_enabled` / `grpc_enabled` / `dbus_enabled`, or `COGNITIVE_MCP_HTTP_DISABLED` etc.), so you can turn HTTP/SSE off and leave gRPC + D-Bus up.

2. Factory CLI, gemini CLI, and claude-code only speak MCP stdio or streamable-HTTP — none of them dial gRPC. So gRPC-as-transport means each CLI's config registers a **stdio shim**: a tiny binary the CLI spawns, which translates MCP JSON-RPC on stdin/stdout → gRPC calls to `10.200.0.1:50052` over the grpc-uplink. That keeps the identity anchor as the WG peer IP and means nothing HTTP-shaped is exposed. No such shim exists yet — `op-mcp-proxy` is LLM-proxy plumbing and `op-grpc-bridge` is domain services, so it'd be a new small bin (op-mcp has a server-side `transport/stdio.rs` you could reuse the framing from).

content.text:
Yes — collapsing `wg-xray` onto the host is the right call, and it solves several of today's problems at once: the two-xray duplicate, the shm-mount-into-container gymnastics, the container reload path, and even the sled mount (the sled already lives on host `/dev/shm` — nothing to mount into a container that no longer exists).

On your transfer idea — let me give you my honest read on the two methods before I design it:

- **btrfs send/receive → yes, for the *data*.** Snapshot the `wg-xray` subvol read-only, `send | receive` to a host staging subvol, then extract the xray config/certs/keys/rumqttd bits natively. It's the safe way to not lose anything you configured in there.
- **Overlay-mask the rootfs onto live host `/` → I'd advise against it.** That container is **Debian trixie**; the host is **Artix**. Overlaying a foreign glibc/coreutils userland over the host root and masking files is a real way to brick the box. We don't need the rootfs — the binaries (`xray`, `rumqttd`) are standalone and already on/pushable to the host (we proved `rumqttd` runs on host). What's actually valuable in there is **config + certs + keys + service defs**, not the OS.

So: **send/receive to staging, cherry-pick the config/certs, run xray + rumqttd as native host s6 services, move the WG addresses to host, then decommission the container.** The one genuinely risky piece is the **networking** — moving `10.0.0.2` (opdbus) and `10.200.0.1` (grpc-uplink) to host interfaces without dropping your remote session — so that gets staged with rollback.

Let me ground the design in what's actually *in* `wg-xray` so nothing's missed:

echo "=== wg-xray network interfaces (what carries 10.0.0.2 / 10.200.0.1) ==="
sudo incus exec wg-xray -- ip -br addr 2>&1 | grep -E "10.0.0.2|10.200.0.1|wg|UP" | head
echo "=== services running in wg-xray (systemd/openrc) ==="
sudo incus exec wg-xray -- sh -c 'systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running --no-pager 2>/dev/null | grep -iE "xray|wg|mq|rumqtt" || rc-status 2>/dev/null | grep -iE "xray|wg" || ps -eo args 2>/dev/null | grep -iE "xray|rumqtt|wg-quick|wireguard" | grep -v grep' 2>&1 | head -15
echo "=== host already has these addrs? ==="

content.text:
Good news — the migration is **far smaller than it looks**, and send/receive turns out to be overkill. The inventory:

- **Only unique content in `wg-xray` = one file**: `/usr/local/etc/xray/config.json` (+ ~22 `.bak-identity` snapshots). **No certs/keys in that dir, no `/etc/ghostbridge/`, no other services** — just `xray.service`.
- **`wg-xray` isn't even carrying `10.0.0.2`/`10.200.0.1` right now** (empty result).
- **The host already has `10.0.0.2`** — on the `opdbus` interface. And **xray already runs on the host** (pid 3599).

So "move everything to host" is mostly *already true by circumstance*. btrfs send/receive would just drag a whole Debian rootfs across to recover **one config file** — not worth it. Let me verify the last unknowns before I commit the design (is the host config the same as the container's, is `10.200.0.1` on host, any certs hiding elsewhere):

input.command:
echo "=== host xray config vs container xray config — same file or different? ==="
sudo incus exec wg-xray -- sha256sum /usr/local/etc/xray/config.json 2>&1
sudo sha256sum /usr/local/etc/xray/config.json 2>&1
echo "=== 10.200.0.1 anywhere on host? ==="
ip -br addr 2>/dev/null | grep -E "10.200" || echo "(10.200.0.1 NOT on host)"
echo "=== any certs/keys ANYWHERE in wg-xray (not just xray dir)? ==="
sudo incus exec wg-xray -- find /etc /root /usr/local -name "*.key" -o -name "*.crt" -o -name "*.pem" 2>/dev/null | grep -viE "ca-cert|ssl/certs|/usr/share" | head
echo "=== what does the container xray config route that the host one might not? (inbound/outbound tags) ==="
sudo incus exec wg-xray -- sh -c 'grep -oE "\"tag\": *\"[^\"]+\"" /usr/local/etc/xray/config.json | sort -u' 2>&1 | head -20
